default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t3-p1.vietnamese: When considering the characteristics of a language, comparing it with another language is a shortcut to understanding. The same applies to Japanese: analyzing Japanese alone will not reveal its true nature. Some characteristics become clear only when Japanese is compared with English. Such comparison is not limited to grammar; similar comparisons can also be made in terms of speech sounds and language use. Comparative research on two languages in this way is called “contrastive language research.” Through this, we also come to understand the characteristics of the features shared by the two languages.
Manners are a way of expressing care and consideration toward the people you interact with and those around you, so as not to make them feel uncomfortable.
Introduces a definition or explanation: マナーとは means “manners are…”.
Marks the people or things an action or attitude is directed toward.
Expresses the aim of avoiding an outcome: so as not to cause discomfort.
Verb dictionary form + ためのものです describes a function or purpose: something intended for doing something.
In Japanese society, there are rules of etiquette for many different situations, but manners are especially valued in business settings.
Sets a context or domain as the topic: in Japanese society; in business settings.
Connects two clauses with a mild contrast: etiquette exists in many settings, but is especially valued in business.
The polite passive form of a する verb: 重視する becomes 重視されます, “are considered important”.
Establishes the focus on business settings, helping identify the intended audience in question 1.
As you pursue your working lives as business professionals from now on, understanding customs unique to Japan and acquiring good manners can be said to help relationships run smoothly and provide a shortcut to success.
Indicates a capacity or role: as business professionals.
Describes an action continuing or developing into the future; 仕事をしていく means pursuing one's working life from now on.
Verb dictionary form + うえで means “when” or “in the course of,” identifying the activity to which the advice applies. It does not mean “after” here.
理解し and スムーズにし use verb continuative forms to connect actions or results; this is not the particle し used to list reasons.
こと nominalizes the actions of understanding Japanese customs and acquiring manners; は makes those actions the topic.
Expresses bringing something into a particular state: 人間関係をスムーズにする means making interpersonal relationships run smoothly.
へ + の modifies a following noun: 成功への近道 means a shortcut to success.
Expresses becoming or serving as something: becoming a shortcut to success.
Presents a conclusion in a measured way: “it can be said that…”.
Directly addresses people entering or pursuing professional working lives, matching the future workers in option 2.

The advice to learn customs unique to Japan makes foreigners about to work at Japanese companies the best fit. Foreigners are inferred rather than explicitly named; success is a benefit, not the main audience clue supporting option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t4-p1.outline.0.no: Defines manners as a way to show care and consideration without causing discomfort to others.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t4-p1.outline.1.no: Narrows the focus from Japanese society in general to business settings, where etiquette is especially valued.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t4-p1.outline.2.no: Advises readers to understand Japanese customs and acquire manners for smoother relationships and success. Together, the clues make option 2 the best match.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t4-p1.vietnamese: Manners are a way of expressing care and consideration toward the people you interact with and those around you, so as not to make them feel uncomfortable. In Japanese society, there are rules of etiquette for many different situations, but manners are especially valued in business settings. As you pursue your working lives as business professionals from now on, understanding customs unique to Japan and acquiring good manners can be said to help relationships run smoothly and provide a shortcut to success.
It is difficult for a large group of people to come together and debate.
Links two actions: people gather and then debate.
Makes the preceding situation the topic of a comment: “the act of … is ….”
People with differing opinions put their views up against one another and debate.
In a clause modifying a noun, の can replace が as the subject marker. 意見の違う modifies 人.
Attaches to a noun to indicate members of a group or a mutual relationship; here, people debating with one another.
Uses the verb's masu-stem to link clauses in written language. ぶつけ links presenting opposing views with 論じる.
Sometimes, people become emotional and criticize the other person's shortcomings.
ときには marks something that happens occasionally rather than all the time.
A noun or na-adjective without な followed by になる expresses a change of state. 感情的になって means “become emotional.”
Links becoming emotional with the subsequent act of criticizing.
Because the person being criticized refuses to budge from their position, the dispute grows increasingly heated.
The passive form of a suru-verb. 批判された means “was criticized” and modifies ほう.
After a modifying clause, ほう identifies one of two sides. Here, ほうが is the noun ほう plus subject marker が, not the advice pattern ～ほうがいい.
States a cause or basis: the dispute intensifies because the criticized side refuses to yield.
An i-adjective with い replaced by く followed by なる expresses a change of state. 激しくなる means “become more intense.”
At such times, try shifting your perspective and looking for strengths in the other person's thinking.
変え is the masu-stem of 変える, linking a shift in perspective with looking for merits in the other person's thinking.
Expresses trying an action. 探してみる means “try looking for”; みる does not mean “see” here.
Directly supports answer 3: shift perspective to consider the merits of the other person's thinking, which means considering their position.
If people go beyond criticizing the other person, find common ground and possible compromises, and discuss things calmly, they can sometimes reach agreement and arrive at a good conclusion.
へ combines with の to modify the following noun and indicate a target. 相手への批判 means “criticism directed at the other person.”
Means “not only … but also ….” Although も is absent here, the sentence adds finding common ground and compromises to criticism.
探し出して links finding common ground and possible compromises with discussing things calmly.
A na-adjective without な followed by に modifies a verb: 冷静に話し合う means “discuss calmly.”
Expresses an “if” condition. 話し合えば is the conditional form of 話し合う.
まとまり is the masu-stem of まとまる, linking reaching agreement with arriving at a good conclusion.
出せる is the potential form of 出す. 結論を出せる means “can reach a conclusion.”
A dictionary-form verb followed by ことがある describes something that sometimes happens. Here, a good conclusion can sometimes be reached; this is distinct from the experience pattern ～たことがある.
Reinforces answer 3: finding common ground and possible compromises requires considering the other person's perspective.
States the benefit of the recommended approach: it can lead to agreement and a good conclusion.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t5-p1.outline.0.no: Discussion is difficult when many people bring differing opinions.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.no: Emotions lead to personal criticism, and the criticized side's refusal to yield intensifies the dispute.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t5-p1.outline.2.no: The author turns to a solution: shift perspective and look for merits in the other person's thinking. This directly supports answer 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t5-p1.outline.3.no: Finding common ground and possible compromises, then discussing calmly, can lead to agreement and a good conclusion.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese: It is difficult for a large group of people to come together and debate. People with differing opinions put their views up against one another and debate. Sometimes, people become emotional and criticize the other person's shortcomings. Because the person being criticized refuses to budge from their position, the dispute grows increasingly heated. At such times, try shifting your perspective and looking for strengths in the other person's thinking. If people go beyond criticizing the other person, find common ground and possible compromises, and discuss things calmly, they can sometimes reach agreement and arrive at a good conclusion.
In today's society, many devices are somewhat difficult for older people living alone to use. I think this is an issue we must consider as society continues to age.
Marks a setting as the topic: 今の世の中には means “in today's society.”
に identifies the people for whom something is difficult; here, older people living alone.
あり is the connective stem of ある, linking clauses in written style, similarly to あって.
Follows a clause to indicate the context of an ongoing process: as society increasingly ages.
Expresses “must” in a formal style. Attach ねばならない to the verb's irrealis stem: 考える → 考えねばならない; する exceptionally becomes せねばならない.
Expresses the writer's thought or judgment: “I think that…”
For example, there seem to be various difficulties: automatic ticket machines are too complicated to use, and LCD television remotes have so many buttons that they are hard to understand.
Expresses an excessive degree leading to the following result. Drop な from a な-adjective or い from an い-adjective: 複雑すぎて and 多すぎて.
使えない is the negative potential form of 使う: “cannot use,” whereas 使わない means “do not use.”
Lists representative examples, implying that there are other cases as well.
Attaches to the verb's ます-stem to express difficulty: 分かりにくい means “hard to understand.”
Expresses an inferred judgment: “it seems that…” The writer presents difficulties they have observed or learned about.
Making devices that are fast and convenient is good, but I hope manufacturers will make more devices that older people, too, can use easily.
The connective form of an い-adjective: 速い → 速くて, linking “fast” with “convenient.”
A dictionary-form verb plus の nominalizes an action; もいいが acknowledges that it is good before shifting to the main point. This is distinct from the permission pattern ～てもいい.
In お年寄りも, も emphasizes that older people should also be able to use the devices easily.
使える is the potential form of 使う, meaning “can use”; 使えるもの means “things that can be used.”
Softly expresses a wish for someone else to do something: 作ってくれないかな conveys “I hope they will make…”
Expresses a thought or wish the writer currently holds.
Direct evidence for option 4: the writer wants more devices that older people can use easily. 使える corresponds to 扱える in the answer.
The writer acknowledges speed and convenience, then uses が to introduce the main wish; this does not establish that those devices already suit older people, as option 1 claims.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.outline.0.la: An issue in an aging society
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.outline.0.no: Many devices are difficult for older people living alone to use, an issue that needs consideration as society ages.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.outline.1.no: Overly complicated ticket machines and television remotes with too many buttons are specific examples, not a conclusion that older people cannot use any devices.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.outline.2.la: A wish for more easy-to-use devices
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.outline.2.no: The writer wants more devices that older people can use easily. This is the main point and the evidence for choosing option 4 in question 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t6-p1.vietnamese:
In today's society, many devices are somewhat difficult for older people living alone to use. I think this is an issue we must consider as society continues to age.

For example, there seem to be various difficulties: automatic ticket machines are too complicated to use, and LCD television remotes have so many buttons that they are hard to understand.

Making devices that are fast and convenient is good, but I hope manufacturers will make more devices that older people, too, can use easily.
Recently, many young people have been taking trips to celebrate their graduation.
To commemorate an event; here, taking a trip to celebrate graduation.
A verb modifies the following noun: 旅に出る若者 means young people who go on trips.
Apparently, among young people who travel abroad, some develop a fever because of overly demanding schedules or shop so much that they go into debt.
Some people within a group fit the description; it does not apply to everyone.
Because of something that causes an unfavorable result: a demanding schedule causes a fever.
Lists representative actions or situations, which need not happen to the same person.
To do too much. しすぎて connects excessive shopping with the resulting debt.
Reportedly; follows a plain form to convey information heard from others. いるそうだ expresses hearsay, not appearance.
Even so, I have no intention of concluding that “young people these days are a sorry lot.”
even so; just because of that
Just because that is so does not mean…; rejects generalizing from negative cases to all young people.
Specifies the content of the following noun: the quotation gives the content of 結論.
Have no intention of doing something; the author does not intend to condemn young people.
In 困ったものだ, conveys an emotionally charged judgment of disapproval or exasperation.
The author rejects condemning young people; this is not a wish for them to avoid criticism, as option 4 suggests.
Surely there are also young people who send postcards from their travels to those who cared for and helped them from childhood through university graduation.
During the period from… to…; here, identifies when the young people received care and help.
A past-tense clause modifies a noun: 世話になった人たち means the people who helped them.
Describes a type or representative example: young people who do things such as sending postcards.
Surely; expresses the author's reasoned expectation, not a verified fact.
This is a positive example the author expects to exist, not a wish that young people send postcards as in option 3.
I think it is a good thing to see the wider world and reassess oneself and one's own country from an outside perspective before entering adult working life.
Before doing something. The verb before 前に takes the dictionary form: 社会に出る前に.
Connects actions: seeing the wider world and then reassessing oneself and one's country.
Attaches to a verb's masu-stem to express doing it again or reconsidering: 見つめ直す means to reexamine carefully.
Nominalizes an action with の and evaluates it: reassessing oneself and one's country is a good thing.
I think that…; marks the author's opinion and helps identify the main point.
Direct evidence for answer 2: the author values reassessing one's country from outside. 見つめ直す corresponds to 見直す in the answer.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t7-p1.outline.0.no: Introduces graduation trips and some cases involving health and money problems. This provides background rather than the author's main opinion.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t7-p1.outline.1.no: The author refuses to condemn all young people based on negative cases and offers an example of gratitude. This helps rule out options 4 and 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t7-p1.outline.2.la: The value of an outside perspective
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t7-p1.outline.2.no: Main opinion: seeing the world before entering adult working life allows people to reassess themselves and their country. This directly supports answer 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t7-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, many young people have been taking trips to celebrate their graduation. Apparently, among young people who travel abroad, some develop a fever because of overly demanding schedules or shop so much that they go into debt.

Even so, I have no intention of concluding that “young people these days are a sorry lot.” Surely there are also young people who send postcards from their travels to those who cared for and helped them from childhood through university graduation. I think it is a good thing to see the wider world and reassess oneself and one's own country from an outside perspective before entering adult working life.
Lately, I feel that young people do not use honorific language very much with their superiors.
Toward…; marks the person an action is directed toward, here one's superiors.
Not very much/often; indicates a low degree or frequency, not complete absence.
Feel that…; presents the writer's subjective impression.
The writer observes that young people use little honorific language, rather than asserting that they use it for communication as option 4 states.
I worry that they may face difficulties once they enter working life.
After…; 社会に出る means entering adult society, usually by starting work.
Worry that something might happen; expresses concern about a possibility rather than denying it.
Concern that young people may struggle at work supports the view that honorific language is necessary in working life.
I think that using honorific language with one's boss at work is natural, and that, to make communication pleasant, one should also use it with colleagues and subordinates whenever possible.
In/at…; 会社では establishes the workplace as the context.
Toward…; here it identifies the boss as the recipient of honorific speech.
It is natural to…; の turns the preceding action into a noun phrase.
And; links statements or reasons, here adding the recommendation to use honorific language with colleagues and subordinates.
In the sense of/with the aim of…; here the aim is pleasant communication.
Also with…; emphasizes that colleagues and subordinates should also receive honorific speech.
Should…; the ta-form here gives advice rather than referring to the past.
I think that…; marks the writer's opinion.
Using honorific language at work is treated as natural, supporting option 2.
The writer recommends using honorific language with colleagues and subordinates too, ruling out option 1's restriction to superiors.
This states the purpose behind the writer's recommendation, not how young people currently communicate as in option 4.
Speaking without honorific language seems likely to help people become closer, but is that appropriate for a working adult?
can become (stem of the potential form なれる)
Without doing…; 使わずに話す means speaking without using honorific language.
If/when…; introduces a possible result of speaking without honorific language.
Seems likely to…; なれそう combines the potential なれる with そう, suggesting that becoming closer seems possible.
But…; shifts from the apparent benefit of omitting honorific language to doubts about its appropriateness.
As…; evaluates the way of speaking from the standpoint of a working adult.
I wonder whether…; a rhetorical question suggesting that speech without honorific language may be inappropriate.
It is speaking without honorific language that seems to promote closeness; option 3 reverses this relationship.
The rhetorical question challenges the appropriateness of omitting honorific language in working life, supporting option 2.
No matter how friendly you are, if you cannot use honorific language, people around you may sometimes keep their distance.
be kept at a distance (in 距離を置かれる)
No matter how…; even great friendliness does not rule out the consequence in the following clause.
If not…; 使えなければ is the negative conditional of the potential 使える, meaning if unable to use.
Be… by…; 周囲の人から identifies the people performing the action in the passive sentence. 距離を置かれる means others keep their distance from you.
Sometimes…; indicates an occasional possibility, not an inevitable outcome.
It gives a concrete consequence of being unable to use honorific language: others may distance themselves. This clearly supports option 2, that it is necessary for a working adult.
I want to master honorific language now, while I still have the chance.
want to acquire; want to master
While there is still…; 今のうちに means now, while the opportunity or favorable circumstances remain. It does not itself establish that the writer is young.
Want to…; expresses the writer's desire to master honorific language.
The writer's desire to learn honorific language reinforces the view that it is an important skill to acquire.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.0.la: Concern about young people's honorific usage
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.0.no: The writer feels that young people use little honorific language with superiors and worries that they may struggle when entering working life.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.1.no: Honorific language is expected with bosses and is also recommended with colleagues and subordinates to make communication pleasant.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.2.no: Although speaking without honorific language may seem to promote closeness, the writer questions its appropriateness for working adults and points out the risk of others keeping their distance.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.3.la: A wish to master honorific language now
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.outline.3.no: The writer concludes with a desire to master honorific language now, reinforcing its importance as a necessary skill.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t8-p1.vietnamese:
Lately, I feel that young people do not use honorific language very much with their superiors. I worry that they may face difficulties once they enter working life.

I think that using honorific language with one's boss at work is natural, and that, to make communication pleasant, one should also use it with colleagues and subordinates whenever possible.

Speaking without honorific language seems likely to help people become closer, but is that appropriate for a working adult? No matter how friendly you are, if you cannot use honorific language, people around you may sometimes keep their distance. I want to master honorific language now, while I still have the chance.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a quality or degree: 暑い → 暑さ (heat).
Expresses an ongoing state or process.
In more than 70 years of life, this is the first time I have experienced such extreme heat.
Follows a quantity to mean that amount or more.
Expresses a process extending from the past to the present; 生きてきて means having lived up to now.
Here, indicates that this is the first such experience in the speaker's lifetime.
This is a first in over 70 years of life, not heat returning after 70 years, so option 3 is incorrect.
While tidying the storehouse, I came across my summer vacation diary from elementary school.
Describes something occurring or being discovered while another action was in progress; this is an actual event, not a hypothetical condition.
In 出てきた, describes an object appearing or coming to the narrator's attention.
Only a few days were recorded as reaching 30 degrees.
と marks the recorded content; 記された is the past passive form of 記す.
Nominalizes the preceding clause and makes it the topic: the days recorded as reaching 30 degrees.
Means only; uses a negative form to emphasize a limited quantity. 数日しかなかった means there were only a few days.
Even so, the diary said that days with temperatures of 30 degrees were very hot.
Expresses what had been written; と introduces the content, and the passive ～ていた describes the recorded state in the past.
Follows a quantity to indicate an approximate value, slightly above or below it.
Indicates that temperatures around 35 degrees are continuing.
If we humans are responsible for this even to a small extent, I think we must make a serious effort to prevent global warming for the sake of our children and grandchildren.
In 少しでも, emphasizes a minimal degree: even a little.
Means if it is the case that; introduces the possibility that humans are partly responsible.
Means for the sake of; 子や孫のために means for the sake of children and grandchildren.
Means must; a formal equivalent of ～なければならない. Attach ねばならない to the negative stem without ない; する exceptionally becomes せねばならない.
Means I think that; expresses the writer's opinion.
Directly states the main message: serious action is needed to prevent global warming. This supports title 1, 温暖化防止.
Children and grandchildren are the beneficiaries and motivation for action, not the overall topic; this rules out option 4.
I do hope to find a way to live making full use of the wind in summer and the sun's blessings in winter.
Sets up parallel, contrasting topics: using wind in summer and the sun in winter.
Links an action to a way of living: living by making use of nature's benefits.
Expresses a heartfelt wish or reflective desire: the writer truly hopes to live this way.
The wish to use nature's benefits in daily life develops the message about preventing global warming, reinforcing title 1.
(Note 1) 土蔵: a storage shed or warehouse.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t9-p1.outline.0.no: The writer introduces abnormal heat experienced for the first time in over 70 years. 初めて differs from 70年ぶり: the heat is not said to be returning after 70 years.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t9-p1.outline.1.no: The childhood diary shows that 30-degree days were rare and already considered very hot; now temperatures stay around 35 degrees. The memories provide background, so option 2 does not cover the whole passage.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t9-p1.outline.2.no: The writer states the responsibility to act for future generations and wishes to use wind and sunlight in daily life. This is the main message, confirming answer 1, 温暖化防止.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t9-p1.outline.3.no: Explains 土蔵 as a storehouse and 真剣 as serious or earnest.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t9-p1.vietnamese:
The abnormal heat continues. In more than 70 years of life, this is the first time I have experienced such extreme heat.

While tidying the storehouse, I came across my summer vacation diary from elementary school. Only a few days were recorded as reaching 30 degrees. Even so, the diary said that days with temperatures of 30 degrees were very hot. Nowadays, temperatures remain around 35 degrees. If we humans are responsible for this even to a small extent, I think we must make a serious effort to prevent global warming for the sake of our children and grandchildren. I do hope to find a way to live making full use of the wind in summer and the sun's blessings in winter.

(Note 1) 土蔵: a storage shed or warehouse.

(Note 2) 真剣: serious; earnest.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.0: The season when food poisoning is likely to occur has arrived.
Attaches to the masu-stem to indicate that something is easy to do or likely to happen. 発生しやすい means “likely to occur.”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.1: That brings my attention to the best-before dates on food.
の nominalizes the preceding clause; the structure identifies the thing in question: “What concerns me is….”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.2: Even with food I bought confidently, believing that the store only displays products within their stated dates, I sometimes carelessly leave it forgotten in the refrigerator and then hurriedly check its best-before date.
で marks the location of an action, while は frames that location as the topic: “in the store….”
The te-form links actions or expresses manner. 期限を守って means “observing the stated time limit.”
The passive combined with ～ている describes the food's state of being displayed for sale.
と marks the content of a thought. The writer buys with confidence because they believe the food is displayed within its stated date.
After a noun, this means “even….” Here it is 食品でも, rather than a verb in the te-form followed by も.
Expresses an unintended outcome, often with regret. しまい is the connective form of しまう.
After a dictionary-form verb, this expresses an occasional occurrence: “sometimes….”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.3: However, for older people like me, the lettering showing the best-before date is small and hard to read, and I often find myself searching in frustration all over the bag—front and back, top and bottom, left and right.
hard to see; hard to read
Gives an example or expresses similarity. 私のような高齢者 means “older people like me.”
Marks the person or group from whose perspective a judgment applies: “for….” は highlights the perspective of older people.
A clause containing a passive verb modifies the following noun: “the lettering in which the best-before date is written.”
Connects an i-adjective to the next description and can indicate a cause. The small lettering makes it hard to read.
Attaches to the masu-stem to express difficulty doing something. 見づらく is the connective form of 見づらい.
Indicates that something also happens frequently. も adds the frequent searching to the difficulty already mentioned.
Direct evidence for Question 1: the writer complains that the lettering is small and hard to read. Option 3, making the lettering larger, addresses this problem.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.4: Why is such important information presented in a way that makes it so inconspicuous?
Describes how something is arranged or its existing state. Here the writer criticizes the inconspicuous presentation without establishing that the manufacturer deliberately hides it.
Expresses wondering or questioning. なぜ～のだろうか means “I wonder why…,” and here also conveys dissatisfaction.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.sentences.5: I want manufacturers to label every food product so that its best-before date is clear at a glance.
Expresses a wish for someone else to do something; に marks that person or group. The writer wants manufacturers to improve the labeling.
Expresses a purpose or desired result: “so that….” 分かるように表示する means “display it so that it can be understood or recognized.”
どの + noun + も means “every…” or “any….” どの食品も refers to every food product.

Directly states the desired outcome: labeling that is clear at a glance. Combined with the complaint about small lettering in sentence 3, this supports option 3. The passage does not request a fixed label position, a different display location, or color coding.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.outline.0.l: Food poisoning season and best-before dates
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.outline.0.n: The arrival of food poisoning season draws the writer's attention to best-before dates.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.outline.1.n: Despite buying confidently, the writer sometimes forgets food in the refrigerator and then hurriedly checks its date.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.outline.2.n: The passage turns to its main problem: older people struggle with small lettering and become frustrated when searching the packaging. This directly supports increasing the lettering size.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.outline.3.n: The writer wants every food product's date to be clear at a glance. Read together with sentence 3, this request corresponds to option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t10-p1.vietnamese:
The season when food poisoning is likely to occur has arrived. That brings my attention to the best-before dates on food. Even with food I bought confidently, believing that the store only displays products within their stated dates, I sometimes carelessly leave it forgotten in the refrigerator and then hurriedly check its best-before date.

However, for older people like me, the lettering showing the best-before date is small and hard to read, and I often find myself searching in frustration all over the bag—front and back, top and bottom, left and right. Why is such important information presented in a way that makes it so inconspicuous? I want manufacturers to label every food product so that its best-before date is clear at a glance.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.0: Recently, when I look around town, I get the feeling that there are more thin women.
When…; here it introduces what the writer notices when looking around town.
The ta-form modifies a noun; 痩せた女性 describes women who are thin.
Have the feeling that…; expresses a subjective impression rather than certainty.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.1: I too began to worry about my figure and tried dieting.
Attaches to a verb's masu-stem to mean beginning to do something; 気になり始め means beginning to be concerned.
Try doing something to experience it or see the result.
A verb's masu-stem can connect clauses in writing; 始め links becoming concerned with trying a diet.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.2: When I reduced how much I ate, my weight did indeed go down.
When…; introduces the actual result of reducing food intake.
Marks a contrast: weight did decrease, but the following sentence describes adverse effects on health.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.3: However, I felt sluggish and also lost my ability to concentrate during class.
The connective form of an i-adjective; だるい becomes だるくて, linking sluggishness with loss of concentration.
Also…; adds loss of concentration to the negative effects of dieting.
Cease to exist or be present; 集中力がなくなる means losing the ability to concentrate.
Describes adverse effects of dieting, supporting the interpretation that the concern is deteriorating health.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.4: I also began catching colds more often.
Nominalizes a verb phrase; 風邪を引くこと means catching colds.
Something also happens more often; here it indicates an increase in the frequency of catching colds.
Catching colds more often is a concrete sign of poorer health after reducing food intake.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.5: I became worried about my health and made a point of eating proper meals; when I did, I quickly recovered.
Become…; 心配になる expresses becoming worried.
Make a conscious effort to do something; here it means adjusting one's habits to eat proper meals.
When…; links eating properly with the resulting recovery.
Recovery after eating properly reinforces the link between reduced food intake and poorer health.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.6: Even I, a high school student, nearly damaged my health, yet recently I have heard that even elementary school children who are still growing are dieting.
Even…; emphasizes that the writer was affected despite already being a high school student.
Attaches to a verb's masu-stem; here it means nearly reaching a state: 壊しかけた means nearly damaged.
Although, and yet…; marks an unexpected contrast with a tone of concern.
Even…; emphasizes the striking case of growing elementary school children dieting.
Expresses an ongoing activity or practice; here it refers to children dieting.
Hear that…; と marks the content of what is heard.
Direct evidence: even the older writer nearly damaged their health, prompting concern that younger children will suffer poor health too. Both questions take option 2.
Identifies the children the writer is worried about: elementary school students who are still growing but already dieting.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.sentences.7: I worry about what will happen to those elementary school children when they reach my age.
When someone has reached/become…; the ta-form marks reaching the age before the point under discussion, not necessarily past time.
Be worried about…; embeds a question as the content of the concern. どうなるのか means what will happen or how things will turn out.
そんな refers to the growing children who are dieting in the preceding sentence, rather than elementary school children in general.
The concern is about the children's health when they reach the writer's age. Together with 体を壊しかけた, this points to 体調を崩すこと, option 2 for both questions.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.outline.0.n: Seeing more thin women leads the writer to worry about their figure and try dieting.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.outline.1.n: Eating less reduces weight but causes sluggishness, poor concentration, and more frequent colds. Proper meals restore the writer's health; this experience underlies the final concern.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.outline.2.n: Since even the high school writer nearly damaged their health, they worry that elementary school children dieting while still growing will suffer poor health as they get older. Both questions take option 2: 体調を崩すこと.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t11-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, when I look around town, I get the feeling that there are more thin women. I too began to worry about my figure and tried dieting.

When I reduced how much I ate, my weight did indeed go down. However, I felt sluggish and also lost my ability to concentrate during class. I also began catching colds more often. I became worried about my health and made a point of eating proper meals; when I did, I quickly recovered.

Even I, a high school student, nearly damaged my health, yet recently I have heard that even elementary school children who are still growing are dieting. I worry about what will happen to those elementary school children when they reach my age.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.0: The other day, we celebrated our 33rd wedding anniversary by going for a drive, something we both love.
A number + 回目 indicates an ordinal occurrence; 33回目 means the 33rd time.
迎え is the connective form of 迎える, linking the marking of an occasion to the following action.
Go out for an activity; ドライブに出かける means to go for a drive.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.1: What is especially enjoyable is chatting in the car.
Nominalizes the preceding phrase with の and identifies the emphasized content: what is especially enjoyable is chatting in the car.
で marks the location of an activity, and の connects it to a noun: chatting that takes place in the car.
The topic sentence directly identifies the pleasure developed in the following sentences, confirming option 4: chatting in the car.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.2: At home, we tend to talk while doing other things, such as watching television or eating.
Sets a location as a contrasting context: at home, as opposed to in the car in the next sentence.
Lists representative actions without implying that they are the only ones.
A verb stem + ながらの + noun describes something occurring while another action is performed, here conversation while watching television or eating.
A verb stem + がちだ expresses a tendency, often an undesirable one; なりがちだ means tends to become.
Provides a contrast: conversation at home accompanies other activities, highlighting the appeal of chatting in the car.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.3: In the car, it is just the two of us, so we can focus on the conversation itself.
After a number of people, indicates that only those people are present; 2人きり means just the two of them.
Follows a noun to emphasize the thing itself.
Can concentrate on something; 集中できる is the potential form of 集中する, and に marks the focus of attention.
States a direct benefit of chatting in the car, supporting the theme in option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.4: From our children and grandchildren to work and life in old age, we never run out of things to talk about.
Lists representative examples, such as children, grandchildren, work, and old age.
Refers to matters concerning the preceding noun.
These are examples of conversation topics; work and old age in option 3 are only part of the discussion, not the overall theme.
Emphasizes the abundance of things to discuss in the car, further developing the main theme.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.sentences.5: Perhaps because we feel relaxed, we can also readily accept each other's views.
Suggests an uncertain cause: perhaps because…; often used with undesirable outcomes, but here the result is positive. ゆとりがある is a verb clause preceding せいか.
A dictionary-form verb + ことができる expresses the ability or possibility of doing something.
Adds another benefit: besides focusing on the conversation, they can also accept each other's views.
Relaxation is presented as a possible reason for better conversation; it does not make a leisurely lifestyle, option 2, the overall theme.
Closes the passage with a benefit of their conversations: being receptive to each other's views.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.outline.0.n: Introduces the couple's 33rd wedding anniversary and their drive, providing the setting for the main topic.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.outline.1.l: The pleasure of chatting in the car
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.outline.1.n: Directly states the passage's theme: chatting in the car is especially enjoyable. This is the main evidence for option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.outline.2.n: Contrasts talking at home while doing other activities with being alone together in the car and focusing on the conversation itself.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.outline.3.n: The couple have many topics to discuss and, perhaps because they feel relaxed, readily accept each other's views. These details explain the appeal of chatting in the car.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t12-p1.vietnamese: The other day, we celebrated our 33rd wedding anniversary by going for a drive, something we both love. What is especially enjoyable is chatting in the car. At home, we tend to talk while doing other things, such as watching television or eating. In the car, it is just the two of us, so we can focus on the conversation itself. From our children and grandchildren to work and life in old age, we never run out of things to talk about. Perhaps because we feel relaxed, we can also readily accept each other's views.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.0: This happened while I was watching a professional baseball game.
Describes an action in progress in the past: the writer was watching the game.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.1: A player on the team I was supporting made an error.
A clause modifies a noun: 応援していた describes チーム as the team the writer was supporting.
Expresses a completed event with regret; here, the player unfortunately made an error.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.2: Then someone supporting the opposing team was heckling the player, shouting, “There's no way you could catch that!”
に marks the person whose ability is discussed. お前に捕れる means “you can catch”; 捕れる is the potential form of 捕る.
A casual form of ～わけがない, expressing strong denial: “there is no way…”.
A casual form of ～だろう. In this jeer, it reinforces a mocking assertion.
Marks a direct quotation; the words inside 「 」 are what the spectator shouted.
Describes an ongoing past action: the spectator was heckling.
Identifies the person performing the action as a spectator supporting the opposing team.
This is the specific action referred to by そういうこと: a spectator heckling the player. Therefore, option 2 is correct.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.3: I play baseball too, but above all, the person those words are directed at must be the most hurt.
Here it describes a regular activity: the writer also plays baseball.
Links clauses with “but,” shifting from the writer's own experience to the feelings of the person being heckled.
The passive form. 言われた is the past passive of 言う and describes the person at whom those words were directed.
Expresses a reasoned expectation: the writer believes the person being heckled must be the most hurt.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.4: I also dislike people who do not observe proper manners.
A negative clause modifies a noun: マナーを守らない人 means “people who do not observe proper manners.”
Means “also,” adding the writer's dislike of people with poor manners.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.5: If they love sports, I would like them to stop doing that sort of thing.
would like someone to do something
Sets a condition: “if they like sports.” With a na-adjective, use 好きなら without だ.
Expresses a wish for someone else to do something; やめてもらいたい means wanting that person to stop the criticized behavior.
Presents the speaker's thought or wish in a softer way.
Refers back to the spectator heckling the player in sentence 2 (zero-based), so the answer is option 2. Option 4 is a broader description of poor manners rather than the specific action described.
Shows that the writer wants the spectator to stop heckling, rather than asking the player to stop making errors.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.6: (Note 1) エラー: a mistake, an error, or a failure.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.sentences.7: (Note 2) ヤジを飛ばす: to criticize loudly by making sarcastic remarks and the like.
Gives an action as a non-exhaustive example. Here, making sarcastic remarks is one way of heckling or criticizing.
Marks manner: 大声で means “in a loud voice” or “loudly.”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.outline.0.l: An incident at a baseball game
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.outline.0.n: A player on the writer's team makes an error, and an opposing supporter heckles him. This action is what そういうこと refers back to.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.outline.1.l: Hurt feelings and a call to stop
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.outline.1.n: The writer believes the target of the jeers is hurt most, expresses dislike of poor manners, and wants sports fans to stop heckling.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.outline.2.n: Defines エラー as an error or mistake and ヤジを飛ばす as loud criticism through sarcastic remarks and similar behavior.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t13-p1.vietnamese:
This happened while I was watching a professional baseball game. A player on the team I was supporting made an error. Then someone supporting the opposing team was heckling the player, shouting, “There's no way you could catch that!”

I play baseball too, but above all, the person those words are directed at must be the most hurt. I also dislike people who do not observe proper manners. If they love sports, I would like them to stop doing that sort of thing.

(Note 1) エラー: a mistake, an error, or a failure.

(Note 2) ヤジを飛ばす: to criticize loudly by making sarcastic remarks and the like.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.sentences.0: Twenty-six students from our sister school in Australia visited my school for a study program, and one female student stayed with my family.
Marks the point of origin: the students came from a sister school in Australia.
学校に marks the destination, while 研修に marks the purpose of the visit.
訪れ is the connective stem of 訪れる, linking the visit to the female student's homestay.
A polite past-tense ending indicating that the homestay took place.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.sentences.1: We were the same age and went to school together for one week.
で is the connective form of だ after the noun 同年齢, linking the shared age to the following event.
Expresses a duration in weeks; 1週間 indicates that they went to school together for one week.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.sentences.2: She took an interest in things such as the many vending machines around town and people dressing their dogs in clothes and taking them for walks.
Nominalizes events with こと and lists examples using や and など; the list is not exhaustive.
Means to take an interest in something; に marks what attracts the interest.
Means to dress someone or an animal in something; 犬に服を着せる means to put clothes on a dog. 着せる is a transitive verb, distinct from the causative form 着させる.
Combines the causative form of a する verb with ～ている. 散歩させている describes having dogs walk, naturally translated here as taking dogs for walks.
These examples show her interest in unfamiliar aspects of everyday life in Japan, providing concrete support for option 3: a country with a different culture.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.sentences.3: I realized that the everyday sights I took for granted were fascinating to people from other countries.
In 見ている, describes sights the narrator regularly sees in everyday life.
私が見ている modifies 当たり前の風景: the ordinary sights that the narrator regularly sees.
Marks a perspective and adds contrast: to people from other countries, those sights are fascinating.
A formal written equivalent of だ or です, used here after the noun こと.
Means to realize that something is true; と introduces the realization. The actual structure here is 興味深いことであると分かりました.
The contrast between ordinary sights for a Japanese person and fascinating sights for foreigners directly reveals different cultural perspectives, supporting option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.sentences.4: Spending time with her made me want to learn more about countries around the world with different cultures.
want to know; want to learn
Means through or as a result of having done something; turns a past experience into the cause of a change in thinking.
In 文化の異なる, の replaces が as the subject marker within a noun-modifying clause: countries whose cultures differ.
Expresses a wish: the verb stem before ます + たいと思う. 知りたいと思いました means that the speaker felt a desire to learn.
The conclusion explicitly identifies cultural differences as the theme, reinforcing option 3; convenience, kindness, and technology are not the main focus.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.outline.0.n: The narrator introduces the Australian students' study visit and a week of going to school with the female student staying at their home.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.outline.1.n: Familiar scenes of daily life in Japan attract the girl's interest. The narrator realizes that ordinary sights can fascinate foreigners, providing the main evidence for option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.l: A desire to explore other cultures
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.n: Time spent with the girl inspires a desire to learn about countries with different cultures, confirming the passage's theme.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
Twenty-six students from our sister school in Australia visited my school for a study program, and one female student stayed with my family. We were the same age and went to school together for one week. She took an interest in things such as the many vending machines around town and people dressing their dogs in clothes and taking them for walks. I realized that the everyday sights I took for granted were fascinating to people from other countries.

Spending time with her made me want to learn more about countries around the world with different cultures.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.0: My older brother, a high school student, had a motorcycle accident in January and spent about five months in the hospital.
To experience an unfortunate event; here, an accident.
Connects successive events: having an accident and then being hospitalized.
Follows a quantity to indicate approximation: about five months.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.1: It was a serious accident that could have killed him, but at the time I felt nothing.
did not think; did not feel
Expresses a possible past state. Here, the accident could have killed him; it does not say that he died.
Connects contrasting ideas: the accident was serious, but the narrator felt nothing.
To feel nothing or be unconcerned. 思わなかった is the past negative form.
The accident was serious and potentially fatal, so it does not support option 2, which says his injuries were minor.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.2: That was because I really hated my brother, who was quick to get angry with me and hit me.
matter; in 僕のこと: me
Follows a person reference to refer to that person; 僕のこと here refers to the narrator himself.
A verb's continuative form links actions. 怒り is the continuative form of 怒る and connects to 手を上げる.
Explains the reason for the preceding statement: he felt nothing because he hated his brother.
Directly states why the narrator felt nothing: he really hated his brother. Option 1 is correct.
Explains his hatred: his brother was quick to get angry and hit him. It does not give the reason in option 3 that his brother was quiet.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.3: After a little while, I began to feel lonely without really knowing why, and the house gradually grew quiet.
After an action or event; here, after a little time had passed.
Expresses a change of state: 寂しい → 寂しくなる; 静か → 静かになる.
Expresses a change progressing over time. なっていった shows the house gradually becoming quiet.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.4: Only after my brother was no longer at home did I realize how important family was.
only then; for the first time
Expresses that a previous state no longer holds. いなくなる means to no longer be present; here, the brother is away in the hospital.
Only after an experience does someone realize something: his brother's absence makes him recognize the importance of family.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a quality or degree: 大切 → 大切さ, importance.
To notice or realize something; に marks what is noticed or realized.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.sentences.5: I felt that having my family in my life meant a great deal to me.
For someone; from that person's perspective.
Thought or felt that…; と marks the content of the narrator's thought.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.outline.0.n: The brother has a serious accident and spends about five months in the hospital. The narrator initially feels nothing because he hates his brother, who gets angry and hits him. This supports option 1; the passage mentions no other brother as suggested in option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.outline.1.n: After a short time, the narrator's feelings change: he begins to feel lonely, and the house gradually grows quiet.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.outline.2.n: His brother's absence leads the narrator to recognize how precious and significant his family is to him.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t15-p1.vietnamese:
My older brother, a high school student, had a motorcycle accident in January and spent about five months in the hospital. It was a serious accident that could have killed him, but at the time I felt nothing. That was because I really hated my brother, who was quick to get angry with me and hit me.

After a little while, I began to feel lonely without really knowing why, and the house gradually grew quiet. Only after my brother was no longer at home did I realize how important family was. I felt that having my family in my life meant a great deal to me.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.0: I return to my hometown on Sado in Niigata Prefecture several times a year.
Several times per time period; 年に数回 means several times a year.
Here it expresses a recurring habit: regularly returning to one's hometown.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.1: On those visits, I often find myself riding the bus from the port with elementary school children on their way home from school.
on the way home from school
A clause modifying a noun: 港から乗るバス means the bus the author boards at the port.
Attaches to an activity noun to indicate that the activity is in progress.
To find oneself together with someone; here, to share the bus with the children.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.2: When the children get off the bus, they always bow to the driver and say, “Thank you very much.”
thank you very much (for what you did)
を marks the vehicle one gets off: getting off the bus.
Dictionary-form verb + とき means when doing something; here, when getting off.
と marks the words accompanying the bow; the children bow while expressing thanks.
The children consistently express gratitude to the driver, illustrating consideration for others.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.3: The driver also responds by saying, “Thank you.”
Also: the driver expresses thanks in return, just as the children do.
To reply with the words quoted before と.
The returned thanks show mutual appreciation, directly supporting the idea of consideration for one another in option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.4: At the crosswalk, the children bowed toward the car that had stopped for them, and once they had finished crossing, they bowed again.
Someone did something beneficial for the person concerned. Here, the car stopped for the children, with the wording conveying appreciation.
To perform an action facing or directed toward someone or something.
Here, し is the connective form of する in おじぎをし, linking the bow to the following action.
Verb stem + 終わる means to finish doing something. 渡り終わる means to finish crossing.
Once/when: introduces the children's bowing again after finishing the crossing.
Describes an action observed in the past; here, the children bowing.
The driver gives way and the children respond with a bow, providing another example of mutual consideration and gratitude.
Bowing again emphasizes gratitude; traffic rules provide the setting rather than the main message.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.5: These moments make me feel truly warm and happy.
An い-adjective changes い to く to connect with the next description: warm and happy.
To come to feel a certain way after witnessing or experiencing something.
The closing emotion shows the author's appreciation of mutual consideration. Together with the preceding examples, it supports option 3, without generalizing about local people's character.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.6: (Note 1) Returning home: going back to one's hometown.
Nominalizes a verb: 帰ること means the act of returning, used here to define 帰省.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.sentences.7: (Note 2) Going home from school: returning home after classes end.
Connects events in sequence: classes end, then one returns home.
Nominalizes the preceding phrase to define 下校.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.outline.0.n: The author introduces regular visits to Sado and bus rides shared with elementary school children returning home.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.outline.1.n: The children thank the driver when getting off, and the driver thanks them in return. This highlights mutual appreciation beyond simply praising the children's manners.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.outline.2.n: The children bow to the car that stops for them both before and after crossing. The focus is consideration and gratitude, rather than an appeal to obey traffic rules.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.outline.3.n: The author's warmth and happiness reveal appreciation for how people treat one another. Taken together, the examples best support option 3: value consideration for one another.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.outline.4.n: Defines 帰省 as returning to one's hometown and 下校 as going home after classes end.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t16-p1.vietnamese:
I return to my hometown on Sado in Niigata Prefecture several times a year. On those visits, I often find myself riding the bus from the port with elementary school children on their way home from school. When the children get off the bus, they always bow to the driver and say, “Thank you very much.” The driver also responds by saying, “Thank you.”

At the crosswalk, the children bowed toward the car that had stopped for them, and once they had finished crossing, they bowed again.

These moments make me feel truly warm and happy.

(Note 1) Returning home: going back to one's hometown.

(Note 2) Going home from school: returning home after classes end.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.sentences.0: Recently, I often see buses with advertisements painted all over their bodies.
A clause precedes and modifies a noun: 広告を描いた modifies バス, describing buses with advertisements painted on them.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.sentences.1: Some have overly flashy designs and colors, and perhaps there are others like me who feel uncomfortable or overwhelmed while riding them.
Lists representative examples without implying an exhaustive list: designs and colors; discomfort and a sense of oppression.
Expresses excess. For a な-adjective, omit な and add すぎる: 派手すぎる means excessively flashy.
あり is the connective form of ある, linking the existence of such buses to the following observation; も means also.
Means like or in the same way as; 私のように means like me.
Attaches to a verb's ます-stem and indicates simultaneous actions or states: using the bus while experiencing discomfort.
Tentatively presents a supposition or opinion: perhaps there are…; might there not be…?
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.sentences.2: Buses that travel all around the city are highly effective for publicity, so I understand why companies place their hopes in this form of advertising.
を marks the space traversed: 街中を走り回る means to travel all around the city.
An い-adjective changes its final い to く to connect clauses: 高い → 高く.
の nominalizes the preceding clause; the expression acknowledges or accepts a point: I understand companies having such expectations.
Identifies the benefit under discussion as the publicity companies expect. This establishes that プラス in the next sentence means benefiting corporate publicity, matching option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.sentences.3: However, if the advertising is far too excessive, it clashes with the cityscape, so I believe it will certainly bring no publicity benefit to the companies.
does not become; does not amount to
States a condition and its consequence: if it is excessive, then…; nouns and な-adjectives take ～だと.
Gives a reason supporting a judgment, often implying other reasons as well: since it also clashes with the cityscape…
決して combines with a negative expression for emphasis: certainly not; by no means.
Means will not become or amount to…; は emphasizes the denied outcome. Here, it means producing no publicity benefit.
と introduces the content of a thought: I think that…
ただ shifts from acknowledging publicity effectiveness to its limitation: excessive advertising may fail to provide the benefit companies expect.

Clashing with the cityscape is a reason the advertising is not beneficial, rather than the definition of プラス. Together with the previous sentence, プラス means providing corporate publicity (option 4), not standing out, fitting the scenery, or entertaining passengers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.sentences.4: That is because I hope the advertisements will blend well with the cityscape and the buses will be loved by a broad range of residents.
Means to harmonize with…; と marks what the advertisements should blend with, here the cityscape.
The passive form of 愛する: to be loved by…; 市民に identifies the residents who love the buses.
Expresses a wish for someone or something else to act or reach a state: wanting the buses to become well loved.
Explains the reason for the preceding opinion: that is because I think or hope that…
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.outline.0.n: The author introduces advertisements covering bus bodies and suggests that overly flashy designs and colors can make passengers feel uncomfortable or overwhelmed.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.outline.1.n: The author understands companies' expectations because buses traveling around the city provide effective publicity. This establishes the benefit referred to by プラス.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.outline.2.n: ただ introduces a qualification: excessive advertising clashes with the cityscape and therefore brings no corporate publicity benefit. The answer to question 1 is option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.outline.3.l: A wish for harmony and well-loved buses
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.outline.3.n: The author explains the wish behind the criticism: advertisements should fit the cityscape and buses should be widely loved by residents. The final note defines PR効果.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t17-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, I often see buses with advertisements painted all over their bodies. Some have overly flashy designs and colors, and perhaps there are others like me who feel uncomfortable or overwhelmed while riding them. Buses that travel all around the city are highly effective for publicity, so I understand why companies place their hopes in this form of advertising. However, if the advertising is far too excessive, it clashes with the cityscape, so I believe it will certainly bring no publicity benefit to the companies.

That is because I hope the advertisements will blend well with the cityscape and the buses will be loved by a broad range of residents.

(Note) PR effectiveness: advertising effectiveness.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.0: In our household, my husband and I write down our menus in a notebook, recording what we ate at each of our three daily meals.
Sets a location or context as the topic: in our household.
Marks an embedded question: 何を食べたか means “what we ate.”
Here it describes an ongoing habit: recording daily menus.
Identifies the daily menu-recording habit, matching 毎日の献立を記録する in option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.1: This is also a way to keep ourselves from forgetting kanji.
Expresses the purpose of preventing something: so as not to forget kanji.
Adds another meaning or purpose: this also serves that purpose.
これ refers to recording menus in the previous sentence and directly connects that habit to remembering kanji.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.2: We both make an effort to use kanji as much as possible and make a habit of looking up unfamiliar characters in a dictionary.
Verb dictionary form or negative form + ようにする expresses a deliberate effort or habit. ようにしています emphasizes maintaining that habit.
A negative clause modifies a noun: 分からない字 means “characters we do not know.”
なるべく corresponds to できるだけ in option 3: using kanji as much as possible when recording menus.
They look up unfamiliar characters; the text does not say they teach each other kanji as option 1 claims.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.3: When I forget to record breakfast or lunch and cannot remember by evening, I occasionally “copy” my husband's notes.
cheat; here, copy the husband's notes
Verb stem + 忘れる means to forget to do something. 書き忘れ is the connective form of 書き忘れる.
Expresses a transition; 夜になって means “when evening comes.”
Introduces a situation meaning “when one cannot/does not…” 思い出せない is the negative potential form of 思い出す.
の replaces a noun understood from context. 夫の here refers to the husband's written record.
Verb dictionary form + こともある means something also happens on occasion. たまに emphasizes its infrequency.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.4: When I can read a kanji in the newspaper that my husband cannot, I silently celebrate, thinking, “Yes!”
A relative clause precedes its noun: 夫が読めない漢字 means “kanji that my husband cannot read.”
Past-form verb + 時は means “when something has happened.” 読めた is the past form of the potential verb 読める.
Marks quoted speech or thought: 「やったー」と conveys the writer's inward exclamation.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.5: Hoping that this will also help prevent dementia, I keep making an effort to continue writing.
Expresses also contributing to an outcome; も adds another benefit the writer hopes for.
Clause + と期待する means to hope or expect that something will happen.
Verb stem + つつ means “while,” often in written language. Here the writer continues writing while holding this hope.
Verb stem + 続ける means to continue doing something. 書き続けています indicates that the writing habit is being maintained.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.sentences.7: (Note 2) 認知症: a condition in which mental responses become slower.
Replace the final い of an i-adjective with くなる to express becoming that way; 鈍くなる means to become slower or less sharp.
Nominalizes the preceding clause to explain the term in the note.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.outline.0.n: The couple records daily menus to remember kanji, making an effort to use them and consulting a dictionary for unfamiliar characters. This supports option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.outline.1.n: The writer describes occasionally copying her husband's notes when she forgets and feeling pleased when she can read a character he cannot.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.outline.2.n: The writer maintains the habit while hoping for the additional benefit of helping prevent dementia.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.outline.3.n: The two notes explain 献立 and 認知症 using the passage's own wording.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t18-p1.vietnamese:
In our household, my husband and I write down our menus in a notebook, recording what we ate at each of our three daily meals. This is also a way to keep ourselves from forgetting kanji. We both make an effort to use kanji as much as possible and look up unfamiliar characters in a dictionary. When I forget to record breakfast or lunch and cannot remember by evening, I occasionally “copy” my husband's notes.

When I can read a kanji in the newspaper that my husband cannot, I silently celebrate, thinking, “Yes!” Hoping that this will also help prevent dementia, I keep making an effort to continue writing.

(Note 1) 献立: menu.

(Note 2) 認知症: a condition in which mental responses become slower.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.0: This happened when I got the time wrong and arrived at a large supermarket nearby an hour before it opened.
Expresses an unintended outcome. 着いてしまった indicates that the writer accidentally arrived too early.
Indicates a time before a reference point; 開店1時間前に means one hour before opening.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.1: As I watched, several dozen people came out through the staff-only entrance.
Introduces something that happens or is noticed while an action is in progress: while watching, the writer saw people come out.
Describes movement toward the speaker or viewpoint; here, people came out from inside into the writer’s view.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.2: Everyone had a bag in hand, and once outside the grounds, they quietly began picking up litter on the road.
は adds emphasis to the location marked by に: everyone had a bag in hand.
The verb stem before ます can connect clauses in written language. 持ち links holding a bag with the following actions.
Here, と marks a sequence: once they were outside the grounds, they began picking up litter.
Verb stem + 始める means to begin doing something. 拾い始める means to begin picking things up.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.3: It must be precisely because of activities like these that the supermarket’s clean appearance is maintained.
Emphasizes a reason: precisely because of. The litter-picking activities are presented as the reason for the supermarket’s clean appearance.
The passive combined with ～ている describes an ongoing maintained state. 保たれている is the passive of 保つ followed by ～ている.
Offers a tentative explanation based on observation: presumably, or it must be that.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.4: Seeing the employees clean and take care of the area outside the store too, I felt a little ashamed of myself: when cleaning around my own home, I had tended to turn a blind eye to the area beyond my property, assuming someone else would take care of it.
pay attention to, take care of
had been turning a blind eye
に + も means “also” or “too.” 店の外にも emphasizes that employees also care for the area outside the store.
In 活動を見て, ～て links an observation to the resulting feeling: seeing the cleaning activities led to feeling ashamed.
だろう expresses a supposition, and と quotes the thought, with “thinking” understood. The writer assumed someone else would clean outside the property.
Means to pretend. 見て見ぬふりをする is an idiom meaning to turn a blind eye; 見ぬ corresponds to 見ない.
Describes an ongoing past action or state; here, it refers to the writer’s previous habit of turning a blind eye.
An い-adjective changes to its く form before なる to express becoming. 恥ずかしくなりました means the writer came to feel ashamed.
Seeing employees care for and clean outside the store prompts the writer to reflect on their own behavior at home.
Direct evidence for option 2: the writer ignored cleaning the road outside their home, assuming someone else would do it. Their own behavior is what causes the shame.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.5: (Note 1) 敷地: land used for constructing a building.
Dictionary-form verb + のに使う means to use something for doing something. Here, のに marks purpose, rather than concession.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.sentences.6: (Note 2) 見て見ぬふりをする: to have seen something but act as though one has not.
A literary or older negative form retained in fixed expressions. 見ぬ means 見ない.
Means to pretend to perform an action or be in a particular state.
Connects contrasting ideas: having seen something but acting as though one has not.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.0.n: The writer arrives an hour before opening by mistake. This sets the scene.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.1.n: Several dozen people emerge through the staff entrance with bags and quietly pick up litter on the road outside the grounds.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.2.n: The writer concludes that these cleaning activities are what maintain the supermarket’s clean appearance.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.3.l: Ashamed of turning a blind eye
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.3.n: The writer feels ashamed for previously leaving the area outside their property uncleaned, assuming someone else would do it. This supports option 2 for question 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.outline.4.n: Defines 敷地 and 見て見ぬふりをする to clarify the area mentioned and the act of turning a blind eye.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t19-p1.vietnamese:
This happened when I got the time wrong and arrived at a large supermarket nearby an hour before it opened. As I watched, several dozen people came out through the staff-only entrance. Everyone had a bag in hand, and once outside the grounds, they quietly began picking up litter on the road.

It must be precisely because of activities like these that the supermarket’s clean appearance is maintained. Seeing the employees clean and take care of the area outside the store too, I felt a little ashamed of myself: when cleaning around my own home, I had tended to turn a blind eye to the area beyond my property, assuming someone else would take care of it.

(Note 1) 敷地: land used for constructing a building.

(Note 2) 見て見ぬふりをする: to have seen something but act as though one has not.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.0: Our home is near the mountaintop, surrounded by nature.
A location clause modifies a noun: the home located near the mountaintop.
Expresses that something is abundant or that a place is full of it.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.1: Perhaps that is why geckos—written here as 「家守」, meaning “house guardian”—have been living here since the house was built about 30 years ago.
kanji spelling of gecko, literally “house guardian”
Perhaps because of…; suggests a possible cause. Although せい often introduces an undesirable cause, here it explains why the geckos settled there.
About; indicates an approximate amount or duration.
Since … ago; marks the starting point of an ongoing situation.
In 住み着いている, describes the continuing state of having settled somewhere.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.2: Recently, their numbers have been increasing.
Describes an ongoing change: the number is increasing.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.3: I was startled when I first saw them, but they did no particular harm, and their movements were endearing.
When something happened; here, when the narrator first saw the geckos.
But…; contrasts the initial surprise with the positive observations that follow.
The past form of an い-adjective: かわいらしい → かわいらしかった.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.4: Believing the traditional saying that they “protect the house for us,” I have watched over them with care for many years.
Someone does something beneficial for the speaker or their group; here, protecting the family's house.
Introduces quoted content modifying a noun, equivalent to ～という＋noun: the saying that…
A written-style connective form: 信じ links to the following clause, similarly to 信じて.
Describes an action continuing from the past up to the present: the narrator has kept watching over them.
Directly states the reason: the narrator believes geckos protect the house. 家 corresponds to 建物 in option 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.5: My grandchild, who loves insects, seems to like geckos too and watches them happily.
Also; the grandchild likes geckos in addition to insects.
Seems…; expresses an inference from observation. で connects it to the next clause.
Do something with an apparent feeling or manner; 楽しそうに見ている means watching with apparent enjoyment.
Describes an ongoing action: watching the geckos.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.6: The geckos clinging to the window glass outside are a treasure, perfect for bringing the family together.
A clause modifies a noun: the geckos clinging to the window glass.
Something ideal or perfectly suited for a purpose; here, bringing the family together.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.sentences.7: (Note) もってこい: the best; perfectly suited.
一番 before an adjective expresses the highest degree: 一番いい means best.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.outline.0.n: The home near the mountaintop is surrounded by nature. Geckos settled there about 30 years ago, and their numbers have recently increased.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.outline.1.n: Initially startled, the narrator came to find them harmless and endearing. The direct reason for cherishing them over the years is the belief that they protect the house, supporting option 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.outline.2.n: The grandchild enjoys watching the geckos, and the narrator sees them as a treasure that brings the family together. This describes their present value, rather than the stated reason for cherishing them over many years.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.outline.3.n: Explains that もってこい means best or perfectly suited.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t20-p1.vietnamese:
Our home is near the mountaintop, surrounded by nature. Perhaps that is why geckos—written here as 「家守」, meaning “house guardian”—have been living here since the house was built about 30 years ago. Recently, their numbers have been increasing.

I was startled when I first saw them, but they did no particular harm, and their movements were endearing. Believing the traditional saying that they “protect the house for us,” I have watched over them with care for many years.

My grandchild, who loves insects, seems to like geckos too and watches them happily. The geckos clinging to the window glass outside are a treasure, perfect for bringing the family together.

(Note) もってこい: the best; perfectly suited.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.0: The polite past form describes a completed event.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.1: Intending to knit a cape and a vest for my grandchild to wear on outings, I borrowed a book from the library to look up measurements and other information.
Lists representative examples without necessarily naming every item.
Expresses an intention to do something for someone else, here knitting clothes for the grandchild.
思い is the connective form of 思う, linking the intention to the following action.
