Modifies a noun by stating its purpose: a book for looking up measurements.
Here it means going somewhere to do something and returning: borrowing a book and bringing it back.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.2: When I opened the book, I found scribbles and folded pages, and I was very shocked.
Introduces a situation discovered upon doing something: opening the book and finding damage.
Describes a resulting state from an earlier action; 落書きしてある means scribbles someone has left.
The passive form: 折られる means to be folded by someone.
Lists representative conditions, such as scribbles and folded pages.
A written-style connective form of ～ている that describes a state and connects it to the next clause.
These examples of damage explain why the author wants readers to take care of library books.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.3: Library books are for everyone to use.
The clause みんなが利用する modifies もの: something that everyone uses.
Gives the reason books must be cared for: they are shared by everyone.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.4: I think any sections that are absolutely necessary can be photocopied.
Expresses possibility or ability; コピーできる is the potential form of コピーする.
Expresses the speaker's thought or opinion.
This is only a suggestion for needed sections, not the overall message about caring for books, so option 1 misses the main point.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.5: With public property, it is important to ensure that everyone can use it comfortably.
利用できる is the potential form of 利用する, meaning to be able to use.
Means taking steps to achieve or maintain a state, here ensuring everyone can use something comfortably.
Nominalizes an action with こと and states that the action is important.
States the central principle of keeping shared property pleasant for everyone to use, supporting option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.sentences.6: I would like everyone to observe basic etiquette.
Expresses a wish for others to do something: wanting everyone to observe etiquette.
Presents an opinion; combined with ～てほしい, it softens the expression of a wish.
Here it emphasizes a minimum standard: basic etiquette should at least be observed.
The explicit closing wish confirms option 4: observe etiquette and take care of library books.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.outline.0.n: After the grandchild's birth, the author borrows a book to look up measurements for knitting clothes.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.outline.1.n: Scribbles and folded pages shock the author, prompting a reminder about how books should be treated.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.outline.2.n: Library books are for everyone; photocopying essential sections is a supporting suggestion, not the main message.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.outline.3.l: Observe etiquette and care for books
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.outline.3.n: The author wants everyone to care for public property so all can use it comfortably and to observe basic etiquette. This main message corresponds to answer 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t21-p1.vietnamese:
My long-awaited grandchild was born. Intending to knit a cape and a vest for my grandchild to wear on outings, I borrowed a book from the library to look up measurements and other information. When I opened the book, I found scribbles and folded pages, and I was very shocked.

Library books are for everyone to use. I think any sections that are absolutely necessary can be photocopied. With public property, it is important to ensure that everyone can use it comfortably. I would like everyone to observe basic etiquette.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.0: This happened in the Kyoto Station building.
Introduces the setting: “This happened at…”. で marks the location of the event, and の connects it to こと.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.1: I saw an elderly woman walking with a pushcart, struggling to open a manually operated door.
で marks the means or aid used; here, the woman walks with a pushcart.
A plain-form clause modifies the following noun: 手押し車で歩く describes おばあさん.
The volitional form plus と expresses intention or effort. 開けようと苦労している means “struggling to open”; する does not appear after と here.
Describes an ongoing action or state: the woman is struggling.
の nominalizes the preceding event; the whole expression means to see that event.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.2: I immediately opened the door for her.
Expresses doing something for someone else; here, the writer opens the door for the elderly woman.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.3: The elderly woman said, “If there were many people like you, Japan would become an even better place,” and gave me a gentle hug.
Expresses similarity: あなたのような方 means “a person like you.”
Expresses a condition, “if…”. いれば is the conditional form of いる.
An い-adjective takes くなる to express change. よくなる means “become better.”
と marks a quotation; 言い is the connective form of 言う, linking the speech to the hug.
Expresses someone doing something for the speaker, conveying appreciation or a sense of receiving kindness.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.4: Through firsthand experience, I truly realized that with just a little kindness, we can all help one another and live happily together.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a quality: 優しい → 優しさ, “kindness.”
Introduces a condition: 優しさがあれば means “if there is kindness”; ほんの少し adds “just a little.”
Marks the people acting together: “all together.”
Attaches to a verb stem to express a mutual action: 助け合う means “help one another.” 助け合い is its connective form.
Expresses ability. An activity noun can take できる: 生活できる means “can live.”
こと nominalizes the preceding content; the expression means to truly feel or realize it.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.5: I plan to enter working life next spring.
A noun plus になる expresses becoming something or entering a new state.
A dictionary-form verb plus 予定です expresses a future plan.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.sentences.6: I vowed to myself that even after entering working life, I would do my part in building a Japan filled with kindness.
go out; enter working life in 社会に出る
Expresses concession, “even if” or “even when.” 社会に出ても means “even after entering working life.”
A noun plus であふれる means “overflow with…” or “be filled with…”. 優しさであふれる modifies 日本.
優しさであふれる日本を作る modifies 一員: a member contributing to the creation of a Japan filled with kindness.
The volitional form plus と心に誓う expresses a firm personal vow. なろう is the volitional form of なる.
Directly states the future goal: to help build a Japan filled with kindness, matching option 1. The goal is not limited to older people, and prosperity and peace are not mentioned.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.outline.0.l: Opening the door for an elderly woman
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.outline.0.n: At the Kyoto Station building, the writer sees an elderly woman struggling with a door and immediately helps her.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.outline.1.n: The woman's words and hug help the writer realize that a little kindness enables people to help one another and live happily together.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.outline.2.n: Preparing to enter working life next spring, the writer resolves to help build a Japan filled with kindness. This supports option 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t22-p1.vietnamese:
This happened in the Kyoto Station building. I saw an elderly woman walking with a pushcart, struggling to open a manually operated door. I immediately opened the door for her.

The elderly woman said, “If there were many people like you, Japan would become an even better place,” and gave me a gentle hug. Through firsthand experience, I truly realized that with just a little kindness, we can all help one another and live happily together.

I plan to enter working life next spring. I vowed to myself that even after entering working life, I would do my part in building a Japan filled with kindness.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.0: I often see students deliberately wearing their uniforms untidily on their way to and from school.
on the way to and from school
Attaches to an activity noun to mean during that activity; 登下校中 means while traveling to and from school.
A clause in the ta-form modifies a noun: 制服をわざと着崩した describes the students being referred to.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.1: They leave the top button of their shirts undone and make their skirts very short, but I oppose wearing uniforms untidily.
外し is the connective stem of 外す, linking undoing a button with keeping the skirt short; it is not the particle し used to list reasons.
Replace an i-adjective's final い with く and add する to express making something have that quality: 短くする means to make shorter.
In 短くしています, this expresses a maintained state: keeping the skirt very short.
Links contrasting clauses: the students' way of dressing and the writer's opposition to it.
A dictionary-form verb plus こと turns an action into a noun phrase; ～に反対です means to oppose it.
Explicitly opposes wearing uniforms untidily, supporting the conclusion that option 2 conflicts with the writer's view.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.2: This is because such clothing is unpleasant for others to look at and appears sloppy.
Expresses a perspective or standpoint: 人から見て means from other people's perspective.
In 気持ちのよい, の replaces が as the subject marker in the phrase modifying もの.
Negates the first description and links it to the next: not pleasant, but sloppy-looking.
An i-adjective changes to its ～く form before 見える to describe appearance: だらしなく見える means to look sloppy.
Gives the reason for the preceding statement, here the opposition to wearing uniforms untidily.
The writer considers how clothing looks to others, so option 1 agrees with the passage and is not the answer.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.3: A friend who dresses that way said, “It's fashionable, and it's nice and cool,” but I cannot agree with the idea that it is enough as long as you yourself are happy with it.
Describes someone's appearance or manner of dress. そんな refers to the untidy clothing described earlier.
Lists reasons or qualities; 流行だし presents being fashionable as one reason and then adds coolness.
The connective form of an i-adjective: 涼しくていい expresses that being cool is pleasant.
Reports a past statement and introduces a contrast. The quotation is the friend's view, while the clause after が is the writer's.
Expresses that meeting a condition is enough. よければ is the conditional form of よい／いい.
States the content of an idea: the idea that personal satisfaction alone is enough.
Expresses inability to agree with something; は highlights the idea the writer rejects.
Direct evidence for option 2: the writer rejects personal satisfaction as sufficient, contradicting the claim that people may dress freely because clothing expresses individuality.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.4: Wearing a uniform properly helps you feel more focused and disciplined and allows you to get the day off to a good start.
make a start (in スタートを切る)
A dictionary-form verb plus ことで expresses a means or cause: by wearing a uniform properly.
引き締まり is the connective stem of 引き締まる, linking two benefits: greater mental focus and a good start to the day.
A dictionary-form verb plus ことができます expresses ability or possibility.
Dressing properly positively affects one's state of mind, so option 4 agrees with the writer and is not the answer.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.5: I also think that a person's character shows in their clothing.
Identifies where or in what aspect a quality becomes apparent; here, character is reflected in clothing.
Follows a plain-form clause to express the speaker's thought or opinion.
States that clothing reflects character, supporting option 3. 人柄 does not imply the freedom to express 個性 asserted in option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.6: (Note 1) Skirt length: the length of a skirt.
Replace an i-adjective's final い with さ to form a noun expressing a degree or quality: 長い → 長さ, length.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.sentences.7: (Note 2) Character: the goodness of a person's nature; moral character.
よい becomes よさ to form a noun meaning goodness; 性質のよさ means goodness of disposition.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.outline.0.n: The writer describes students wearing untidy uniforms and objects because the appearance is sloppy and unpleasant to others. This also shows that option 1 agrees with the passage.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.outline.1.n: The friend's remarks contrast with the writer's view. The writer rejects the idea that personal satisfaction alone is enough; since the question asks for the conflicting view, the answer is 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.outline.2.l: Benefits and significance of dressing neatly
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.outline.2.n: Dressing neatly promotes mental focus and a good start to the day, and clothing reflects character. These points support options 4 and 3 respectively.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.outline.3.n: Explains スカート丈 as skirt length and 人柄 as a person's nature and character.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t23-p1.vietnamese:
I often see students deliberately wearing their uniforms untidily on their way to and from school. They leave the top button of their shirts undone and make their skirts very short, but I oppose wearing uniforms untidily. This is because such clothing is unpleasant for others to look at and appears sloppy. A friend who dresses that way said, “It's fashionable, and it's nice and cool,” but I cannot agree with the idea that it is enough as long as you yourself are happy with it.

Wearing a uniform properly helps you feel more focused and disciplined and allows you to get the day off to a good start. I also think that a person's character shows in their clothing.

(Note 1) Skirt length: the length of a skirt.

(Note 2) Character: the goodness of a person's nature; moral character.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.0: I was born with a disability in my legs and use a wheelchair in daily life.
あり is the connective form of ある, linking the condition of having a disability to the following information.
Marks a means: 車いすで means using a wheelchair.
Describes an ongoing state or habitual way of life.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.1: From my wheelchair, I often cannot see things that my friends can see.
be visible; appear before one's eyes
Sets a condition involving a position or viewpoint: when viewed from…. Here, から marks the viewpoint, not a reason.
は highlights the contrast between what is visible to the friends and what is visible to the narrator.
The preceding clause modifies もの: things that are visible.
Often there are times when something does not happen; describes a recurring situation, unlike the experience pattern ～たことがある.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.2: That used to bother me terribly.
unbearably; extremely (in this emotional emphasis pattern)
Follows a な-adjective to express an intense, uncontrollable feeling. 嫌で仕方がありませんでした means it used to feel terribly unpleasant, rather than making a separate statement that there was no alternative.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.3: But after I became a university student, my way of thinking changed a little.
A noun followed by になる means to become…. The て-form connects this to the subsequent change.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.4: As I travel along the road in my wheelchair, I can also discover little flowers that people pass by without noticing.
be walking; here, moving in a wheelchair
end up being passed by unnoticed
を marks a route or area of movement: 道を歩く means to travel along a road. In this context, the narrator is using a wheelchair.
While doing…; introduces something noticed during an ongoing activity.
The passive form of a する-verb. 素通りされる modifies 花: flowers that people pass by without noticing.
Expresses an eventual outcome, often with a sense of regret; here, the flowers end up overlooked.
Can also…; も emphasizes an additional possibility offered by the wheelchair viewpoint.
Provides an explanation for the change in the narrator's thinking.
Gives a concrete example of what can be noticed from a wheelchair, showing the value of the one-meter-high viewpoint.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.5: I think there may also be a world that my friends cannot see.
A dictionary-form verb followed by ことができない expresses inability to do something.
There is also…; adds that the narrator has a distinct world available to their own view.
I think perhaps…; presents a tentative view rather than a negative assertion.
Summarizes the discovery that the narrator's viewpoint reveals things friends cannot see, reinforcing the theme of the world viewed from a wheelchair.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.6: The world one meter above the ground is not bad either.
Means also or either: the narrator acknowledges value in the world viewed from a height of one meter.
The polite negative form of an い-adjective. 悪くない conveys a mildly positive assessment: not bad.
The conclusion directly states the central image and the narrator's new positive attitude. Therefore, the best title is option 3: 地上1メートルの世界.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.sentences.7: (Note) 素通りする: here, it means to pay no attention.
pass straight by; here, pay no attention
Limits the scope of the explanation: ここでは means in this context.
Means…; used to explain the meaning of a word or expression.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.0.l: A viewpoint that once caused frustration
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.0.n: The narrator introduces their wheelchair use and the frustration of being unable to see things their friends can see. それ in sentence 2 refers to the situation described in sentence 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.1.n: でも marks the turning point: after entering university, the narrator begins to view their situation differently.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.2.n: Small flowers overlooked by others illustrate the value of the wheelchair viewpoint. The narrator realizes that they too can see things their friends cannot.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.3.l: The world one meter above the ground
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.3.n: The conclusion captures the message of accepting and appreciating one's own viewpoint, establishing option 3 as the answer. Option 1 is too broad, option 2 centers on the friends, and option 4 suggests an invisible world that the passage does not describe.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.outline.4.n: Explains the contextual meaning of 素通りする: to pay no attention.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t24-p1.vietnamese:
I was born with a disability in my legs and use a wheelchair in daily life. From my wheelchair, I often cannot see things that my friends can see. That used to bother me terribly.

But after I became a university student, my way of thinking changed a little. As I travel along the road in my wheelchair, I can also discover little flowers that people pass by without noticing. I think there may also be a world that my friends cannot see. The world one meter above the ground is not bad either.

(Note) 素通りする: here, it means to pay no attention.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.0: Since this spring, I have been serving as a class representative in the PTA for my second daughter, who is in the middle-year kindergarten class.
middle-year kindergarten class, usually for four-year-olds
Marks a starting point: この春から means “since this spring.”
A clause modifying a noun: 幼稚園年中組にいる identifies the class the second daughter attends.
Describes an ongoing role or activity.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.1: States a quantity, with the final だ omitted. 1クラス4人 means four people per class.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.2: Including the time when my eldest daughter attended, this is already my fifth time serving in this role.
Nominalizes an action with の and gives information about it: serving in this role is now the speaker’s fifth time.
Means “including…” or “if we count…too,” specifying what is included in the total.
Marks the ordinal number of an occurrence: 5回目 means “the fifth time.”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.3: Previously, we communicated with representatives from other classes and others by email, but we agreed to meet and talk in person whenever possible from now on, and have had about three discussions over lunch.
との links the people contacted to 連絡; など indicates that other similar people are included.
で marks the means, while ～ていた describes a past practice: communicating by email.
Connects contrasting ideas: past use of email and a new preference for meeting in person.
Expresses an agreed decision to do something. 話そうということになり means they agreed to talk, with なり connecting to what followed.
Follows a quantity to indicate approximation: 3回ほど means “about three times.”
Combines purposes or activities: having a discussion while also having lunch.
Shows an agreement to meet whenever possible, without saying email was completely abandoned; rules out option 2.
Identifies the discussions over lunch mentioned in the question; the next sentence gives the reason.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.4: This was because the wording and expressions used in emails had sometimes caused misunderstandings or been perceived as unpleasant.
Marks a cause: the wording and phrasing in emails led to misunderstandings or unpleasant impressions.
Lists representative events without implying that they happened in sequence or at the same time.
The passive form of 思う means being thought of or perceived in a certain way. 不快に思われる means being perceived as unpleasant.
Describes something that had happened before: here, previous problems with email communication.
Gives the reason for the preceding statement. This directly signals the evidence for a question asking why.
Directly explains the meetings: emails had caused misunderstandings or unpleasant impressions. This supports option 3, because the intended meaning may not come across correctly in email.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.5: As mobile phones have become widespread, calling and emailing have become more convenient, but I felt that meeting and talking in person is also important.
Marks a cause: the widespread adoption of mobile phones.
Expresses a change of state. A な-adjective takes に before なる: 便利になる means “become convenient.”
Acknowledges the convenience of calls and emails while emphasizing that meeting in person also matters.
Nominalizes an action: 会って話すこと means “meeting and talking in person.”
Introduces what the writer felt or realized: “I felt that…”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.6: (Note 1) 年中組: Refers to a kindergarten class usually made up of four-year-old children.
Means “consist of” or “be made up of”; here it describes the class membership.
Means “refer to” or “denote,” often used to define a term.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.sentences.7: (Note 2) PTA: An association consisting mainly of students’ parents and teachers.
Modifies a noun by specifying its composition: an association made up of students’ parents and teachers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.outline.0.n: The writer serves as a class representative in her second daughter’s PTA. Each class has four representatives, and this is her fifth time, including her eldest daughter’s years. This experience is background information, not the reason for the lunch discussions.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.outline.1.l: Meeting in person to avoid misunderstandings
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.outline.1.n: After communicating by email, the group agreed to meet whenever possible and held about three discussions over lunch. Emails had caused misunderstandings or unpleasant impressions, so the answer to question 1 is option 3. The passage does not say that conversation would be more enjoyable or that email was completely abandoned.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.outline.2.n: The writer concludes that although calling and emailing are convenient, meeting and talking in person is also important.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.outline.3.n: Defines 年中組 as a kindergarten class usually for four-year-olds and PTA as an association mainly comprising students’ parents and teachers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t25-p1.vietnamese:
Since this spring, I have been serving as a class representative in the PTA for my second daughter, who is in the middle-year kindergarten class. Each class has four representatives. Including the time when my eldest daughter attended, this is already my fifth time serving in this role.

Previously, we communicated with representatives from other classes and others by email, but we agreed to meet and talk in person whenever possible from now on, and have had about three discussions over lunch. This was because the wording and expressions used in emails had sometimes caused misunderstandings or been perceived as unpleasant.

As mobile phones have become widespread, calling and emailing have become more convenient, but I felt that meeting and talking in person is also important.

(Note 1) 年中組: Refers to a kindergarten class usually made up of four-year-old children.

(Note 2) PTA: An association consisting mainly of students’ parents and teachers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.0: I returned to my hometown during summer vacation.
Marks when something happens: 夏休みに means during summer vacation.
Return to a place; に marks the destination.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.1: The purpose of my visit home was to see my grandfather, who had fallen seriously ill in April and was still in the hospital.
visit to someone who is ill
A plain-form verb modifies a noun: 帰る目的 means the purpose of returning.
Marks a cause: 重い病気で倒れ means falling ill due to a serious illness.
The continuative form 倒れ connects to the following clause, much like 倒れて.
In 今も, indicates that the situation continues even now.
Attaches to an activity noun to indicate an ongoing state: 入院中 means currently hospitalized.
The plain past form of だ, used here to describe the purpose of the trip home.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.2: My grandfather had become very thin, and even when I called out to him, he could barely manage to look toward me. It pained me to see him like that.
Connects states or events: 痩せて links his weight loss to the description that follows.
Even if or even when; despite being called, the grandfather could respond only slightly.
Can barely manage to do something; here, looking toward the narrator was all he could manage.
The connective form of だ after 状態 links the grandfather's condition to the narrator's emotional response.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.3: I grew up in my grandparents' care.
Receive someone's care or help; に marks the person providing it.
Describes the circumstances of growing up: growing up while being cared for by one's grandparents.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.4: Thanks to my grandparents, I did not feel lonely as a young child and was also able to learn many different things.
help or benefit behind a good outcome
Thanks to; introduces the cause of a positive outcome and often expresses gratitude.
Experience a feeling; 寂しい思いをする means to feel lonely.
A negative connective meaning without doing or not doing; する becomes せず. Here it links not feeling lonely with learning many things.
Past potential form: 学ぶ → 学べる → 学べた, meaning was able to learn.
Shows the benefits the narrator received from grandparents, supporting option 2. The person who avoided loneliness was the narrator as a child, not the grandparents as in option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.5: It is said that many households in Japan today are nuclear families, but I want to raise my children together with my own parents.
nuclear family, typically parents and their children
Reports what is said or heard: many households are said to be nuclear families.
Connects contrasting ideas: the prevalence of nuclear families and the narrator's wish to raise children with their parents.
Together with someone; 親 refers to the narrator's parents, who would be the children's grandparents.
Expresses the speaker's wish: 子育てをしたい means wanting to raise children.
The narrator contrasts nuclear families with a wish to involve their own parents in child-rearing, showing a preference for grandparents' involvement and supporting option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.sentences.6: That is because I want my children to grow up receiving their grandparents' love, just as I did.
Expresses a wish for someone to do something or experience a certain state. に marks that person, while は highlights 子ども.
Like or just as; 自分のように means just as the narrator did as a child.
Describes the experience of growing up: 愛を受けて育つ means growing up receiving love.
It is because; explains the reason for wanting to raise children with one's parents in the preceding sentence.

Direct evidence: the narrator wants children to grow up with their grandparents' love. Among the choices, option 2 matches this view; the reason concerns the children's benefit, not the grandparents' loneliness.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.outline.0.l: Returning home to visit an ill grandfather
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.outline.0.n: The narrator returns home during summer vacation to visit a hospitalized grandfather and feels distressed by his weakened condition.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.outline.1.n: The narrator grew up in grandparents' care, avoided loneliness, and learned many things. This experience underlies the narrator's view of child-rearing.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.outline.2.n: Although nuclear families are common, the narrator wants to raise children with their own parents so the children can receive grandparents' love. This is the main support for option 2: nuclear families are not desirable for children.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t27-p1.vietnamese:
I returned to my hometown during summer vacation. The purpose of my visit home was to see my grandfather, who had fallen seriously ill in April and was still in the hospital. He had become very thin, and even when I called out to him, he could barely manage to look toward me. It pained me to see him like that.

I grew up in my grandparents' care. Thanks to them, I did not feel lonely as a young child and was also able to learn many different things. It is said that many households in Japan today are nuclear families, but I want to raise my children together with my own parents. That is because I want my children to grow up receiving their grandparents' love, just as I did.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.0: During a break in a university lecture, students sometimes approach their teacher and say, “I don’t get it, so tell me.”
Gives a reason: the student asks for an explanation because they do not understand.
The te-form makes a casual request; 教えて lacks appropriate politeness toward the teacher here.
と marks the quoted words used when addressing someone.
Expresses that something happens on some occasions.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.1: They speak as if talking to a friend, which makes me feel that this is rather rude.
Modifies a noun through comparison: language like that used with friends.
Expresses a tentative judgment, roughly “I feel that this may be…”; here the speaker judges the language to be rude.
The judgment that the language is rude supports embarrassment as a likely consequence of failing to improve it.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.2: Even at the shops where they work part-time, some students speak rudely to customers.
do; use a manner of speaking
Means “even at…,” extending the example from the classroom to a part-time workplace.
Means “toward”; a connective form of に対して that identifies the target of an action.
Attaches to a verb’s masu-stem to express a way of doing something; 話し方 means “way of speaking.”
Speaking rudely to customers illustrates behavior that could cause embarrassment in a work setting.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.3: Young people today are often criticized for not knowing honorific language, but given this behavior, such criticism is understandable.
Means “be criticized for…”; と introduces the criticism and される is passive.
Links contrasting ideas: criticism exists, but the writer considers it justified.
Means “given…, it is understandable”; これ refers to the impolite speech described earlier.
Expresses the writer’s conjecture or judgment: probably; presumably.
Being criticized for not knowing honorific language supports choosing embarrassment in the concluding sentence.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.4: As someone of the same generation, I find this regrettable.
Means “as…” and identifies the writer’s position as someone of the same generation.
Expresses a feeling or assessment; 残念に思う means “find regrettable.”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.5: If students do not refine their manner of speaking while still at university, they will probably feel (　　) when they enter working life.
Means “while still…” and identifies the period within which the improvement should take place.
Means “if not…”; replace the final い of the nai-form with ければ: 磨かない → 磨かなければ.
Means “when one has become…”; the ta-form marks becoming a working adult as completed before the resulting experience, rather than necessarily referring to the past.
Means “experience a … feeling”; the adjective before 思い specifies it, as in はずかしい思いをする, “feel embarrassed.”
Predicts a likely consequence: will probably…
Sets up a failure to improve one’s speech as a student, leading to a negative consequence in working life.

Choose 4, はずかしい: rude speech that attracts criticism can cause embarrassment in working life. うれしい expresses happiness and なつかしい nostalgia; くるしい expresses distress and fits the focus on social manners less closely.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.sentences.6: (Note) ぞんざい: an impolite manner.
Negates a noun or na-adjective; 丁寧ではない means “not polite.”
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.outline.0.n: The writer describes students addressing teachers casually and judges this manner of speaking to be rude.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.outline.1.n: The part-time workplace example shows the same problem in customer interactions. The writer finds criticism of young people’s lack of honorific language understandable and regrets it as a member of the same generation.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.outline.2.l: Refine speech while still a student
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.outline.2.n: The conclusion predicts that failing to refine one’s speech as a student will lead to embarrassment in working life. The best completion is はずかしい, option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.outline.3.n: Explains ぞんざい as an impolite manner.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t28-p1.vietnamese:
During a break in a university lecture, students sometimes approach their teacher and say, “I don’t get it, so tell me.” They speak as if talking to a friend, which makes me feel that this is rather rude.

Even at the shops where they work part-time, some students speak rudely to customers. Young people today are often criticized for not knowing honorific language, but given this behavior, such criticism is understandable. As someone of the same generation, I find this regrettable.

If students do not refine their manner of speaking while still at university, they will probably feel (　　) when they enter working life.

(Note) ぞんざい: an impolite manner.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.0: Currently, in the city where I live, the light from the ground is so bright every night that the night sky is not dark enough.
Expresses an ongoing state: 住んでいる means living somewhere.
In 私の住んでいる都市, の replaces が as the subject marker within a relative clause: the city where I live.
Connects an i-adjective to the following clause; here it expresses a cause.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a degree or quality: 暗い → 暗さ, darkness.
Identifies excessive ground-level light as the cause. Together with the wish in sentence 6, this implies reducing that light, supporting option 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.1: As a result, only a single star is visible.
Introduces the result of the situation just described.
Expresses limitation: just one star is visible; たった emphasizes how few there are.
そのため links excessive light in sentence 0 to the visibility of just one star, reinforcing the need to reduce ground-level light.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.2: The glittering stars filling the sky cannot be seen at all.
Used with a negative form to mean not at all.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.3: In my hometown, where I was born, the twinkling of the stars is clearly visible in the perfectly clear night sky.
私の生まれた modifies 故郷; の marks 私 as the subject and can be replaced by が.
Marks a location as the topic, contrasting the hometown with the city.
Added to a verb stem to express completeness; 澄み切った means perfectly clear.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.4: Children in earlier times would gaze at the stars and experience nature at night.
Uses the verb stem to connect actions in written language; 眺め functions like 眺めて.
Looks back on an action or experience that has continued or accumulated over time up to the reference point.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.5: What are children today to do when they have no night sky to look up at?
Describes someone or something lacking something; の replaces が within the relative clause.
Expresses a suitable course of action; どうすればいい asks what one should do.
Expresses the writer's wondering or concern rather than directly requesting an answer.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.6: I pray that someone will find a way to improve things so that children in the city, too, can see glittering stars in the night sky they look up at.
Combines the location marker に with も, meaning also in the city's night sky.
見られる is the potential form of 見る here, meaning can see, rather than a passive form.
After a potential form, expresses a desired outcome: so that the stars can be seen.
Expresses a prayer that someone will do something helpful. と marks the content of the wish; the person is unspecified.
States the desired outcome: city children should also see stars. Combined with the cause in sentences 0–1, this supports option 1: reducing ground-level light.
The writer hopes someone will improve the situation; the specific measure is inferred from the opening cause rather than explicitly stated here.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.7: (Note 1) きらめく: for the sun or stars to shine with a sparkle.
Lists representative examples without making the list exhaustive.
と follows the mimetic word きらきら to describe how something shines.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.sentences.8: (Note 2) 澄み切る: a state in which the sky has no cloudiness or the like and is exceptionally clear.
Marks examples: cloudiness and similar conditions.
The connective form of ない, linking the absence of cloudiness to the clear state that follows.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.0.n: Ground-level light prevents the sky from becoming dark enough, leaving only one star visible. This cause supports reducing the light, as stated in option 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.1.l: The hometown sky and past experiences
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.1.n: The writer contrasts the city sky with the clear hometown sky and recalls how children in earlier times experienced nature by watching the stars.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.2.n: The rhetorical question expresses concern about children losing the opportunity to enjoy the night sky; it does not mean the sky has literally disappeared.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.3.l: A wish for city children to see stars
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.3.n: The writer hopes conditions will improve so city children can also see stars. Together with the opening cause, this yields option 1: reducing ground-level light.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.outline.4.n: Defines きらめく and 澄み切る. The note about the sky's clarity does not support choosing the air-cleaning option.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t29-p1.vietnamese:
Currently, in the city where I live, the light from the ground is so bright every night that the night sky is not dark enough. As a result, only a single star is visible. The glittering stars filling the sky cannot be seen at all. In my hometown, where I was born, the twinkling of the stars is clearly visible in the perfectly clear night sky. Children in earlier times would gaze at the stars and experience nature at night. What are children today to do when they have no night sky to look up at?

I pray that someone will find a way to improve things so that children in the city, too, can see glittering stars in the night sky they look up at.

(Note 1) きらめく: for the sun or stars to shine with a sparkle.

(Note 2) 澄み切る: a state in which the sky has no cloudiness or the like and is exceptionally clear.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.0: Dictionary-form verb + ことが大好きだ means to love doing something. こと nominalizes 歌う.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.1: Three years ago, I sang a song as a gift at my cousin’s wedding.
Marks the place or occasion of an action, here the wedding.
Means to have given something as a gift; here, 歌をプレゼントした means singing a song as a gift.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.2: Although I have no particular talent for singing, tears welled up in the eyes of my cousin, relatives, and grandparents, and I realized they were listening intently to me.
Means “it is not the case that…” and rejects a possible assumption. Here, the writer denies having any particular singing talent.
Connects contrasting clauses: despite having no particular talent, the writer moved the listeners.
Lists representative examples without necessarily giving an exhaustive list.
あふれ is the continuative form of あふれる, linking the tears welling up to the following clause.
Describes an ongoing action done for the speaker, conveying appreciation for the listeners’ attention.
Means “realized that…”; の nominalizes the preceding clause.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.3: At that moment, I truly felt the tremendous power and potential of music.
A clause modifying a noun: 音楽が持つ力 means “the power that music possesses.”
Replace the final い of an い-adjective with さ to form a noun expressing a quality or degree: すごい → すごさ.
Lists aspects the writer experienced: music’s tremendous power and its potential.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.4: I am currently studying nursing at university.
Sets the present as the topic, shifting from a past experience to current studies.
Marks where the studying takes place: at university.
Means to be studying a particular field; ～ている describes an activity continuing during the present period.
Establishes that the writer studies nursing, supporting the nursing career in option 2 rather than the physician role in option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.5: In recent years, music therapy and similar approaches have been receiving attention, but I think more music could be played in hospital rooms.
Presents examples within a broader group: music therapy and similar approaches.
Combines the passive with ～ている to describe something currently receiving attention.
Links the background to a mildly contrasting opinion: although music therapy receives attention, the writer would welcome more music in hospital rooms.
Means “may…” or “it would be fine if…”; here, it gently suggests that more music in hospital rooms would be welcome.
Means “I think that…” and marks the writer’s personal opinion.
Shows the writer’s interest in bringing music into patient care settings, supporting option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.sentences.6: I too am working hard every day, hoping that someday I can share the joy of activities such as singing with patients.
Gives an action as an example while implying other activities. 歌ったりする means doing things such as singing.
The preceding clause modifies 楽しみ: 患者さんと歌ったりする楽しみ is the joy of doing things such as singing with patients.
分かち合う → 分かち合える (can share) → 分かち合えれば (if one can share): the potential form combined with the ～ば conditional.
Expresses “I hope…” or “it would be nice if….” いいな conveys the writer’s wish rather than advice.
Attaches to the ます-stem: 思いながら. The writer works hard each day while keeping this hope in mind.
Describes an ongoing activity; together with 日々, it indicates sustained daily effort.
Expresses the wish to share the joy of singing with patients. Combined with studying nursing in sentence 4, this is the main evidence for option 2: using music in nursing work.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.0.l: A love of singing and a wedding gift
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.0.n: The writer introduces a love of singing and recalls singing as a gift at a cousin’s wedding three years earlier.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.1.n: The relatives’ emotional response and attentive listening lead the writer to experience music’s power and potential firsthand.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.2.n: The focus shifts to the present: the writer studies nursing and would welcome more music in hospital rooms. This establishes the professional field and area of interest.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.3.l: Hoping to share joy with patients
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.outline.3.n: The wish to sing with patients motivates the writer’s daily effort. Together with the nursing studies, this supports option 2: intending to use music in nursing work.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t30-p1.vietnamese:
I love singing. Three years ago, I sang a song as a gift at my cousin’s wedding. Although I have no particular talent for singing, tears welled up in the eyes of my cousin, relatives, and grandparents, and I realized they were listening intently to me. At that moment, I truly felt the tremendous power and potential of music.

I am currently studying nursing at university. In recent years, music therapy and similar approaches have been receiving attention, but I think more music could be played in hospital rooms. I too am working hard every day, hoping that someday I can share the joy of activities such as singing with patients.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.0: At last, a season with pleasant weather has arrived.
Attaches to the verb stem before ます to mean easy to do. 過ごしやすい describes comfortable living conditions.
Noun + になる expresses a change of state; here, the arrival of a pleasant season.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.1: Recently, one morning when I got up and opened the window, the fragrance of sweet osmanthus drifted into my room.
Introduces background information gently; it does not express a strong contrast here.
Links actions in sequence: getting up and then opening the window.
After a dictionary-form verb, indicates that something happened or was noticed upon performing an action.
Expresses movement toward the speaker: the fragrance drifts into the room from outside.
The triggering event was opening the window and experiencing the osmanthus fragrance. This directly supports option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.2: I find it very difficult to get up in the morning.
Dictionary-form verb + のが苦手 expresses difficulty with an activity or being poor at it. It does not necessarily mean hating it.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.3: However, the fragrance of sweet osmanthus became my only morning pleasure.
pleasure, something to look forward to
Noun + になる expresses a change: the fragrance became a morning pleasure.
Shows that the fragrance itself provided motivation to get up in the morning, reinforcing option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.4: I came to enjoy getting up in the morning.
Dictionary-form verb + のが好き expresses liking an activity; の turns the action into a noun phrase.
A な-adjective without な + になる expresses a change of state. 好きになりました means came to like.
Confirms the change after the fragrance became a pleasure: the writer came to enjoy getting up in the morning.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.5: The sky is beautiful, and I can also feel that I am alive.
Lists related points or reasons. A な-adjective takes だし in the present affirmative form.
In 生きている, expresses the ongoing state of being alive.
んだ emphasizes realization, な adds a reflective feeling, and と marks what is felt: the awareness of being alive.
Dictionary-form verb + ことができる expresses ability; replacing が with も adds the meaning also.
This is an additional feeling experienced after coming to enjoy mornings, rather than the initial cause, so option 3 is incorrect.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.sentences.6: I feel it was such a missed opportunity, wondering why I had not been able to wake up every morning surrounded by the beautiful sky and the fragrance of flowers.
The passive form of 包む, meaning to be surrounded or enveloped by something.
Verb stem before ます + ながら expresses simultaneous actions or states: waking up while surrounded by the sky and floral fragrance.
The past negative potential form of an ichidan verb: 起きる → 起きられる → 起きられなかった, meaning could not get up.
Marks the question the writer is reflecting on: why they had not been able to wake up that way before.
Expresses a current feeling. もったいない思いがしています conveys regret over a missed opportunity.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.outline.0.n: A pleasant season has arrived. One morning, the writer opens the window and experiences osmanthus fragrance drifting into the room, triggering the later change.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.outline.1.n: Although getting up in the morning was difficult, the writer came to enjoy it because the fragrance became a morning pleasure. This sequence reinforces option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.outline.2.n: The writer enjoys the beautiful sky, feels alive, and regrets previously missed mornings. Feeling alive follows the change, so option 3 does not identify the initial cause.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
At last, a season with pleasant weather has arrived. Recently, one morning when I got up and opened the window, the fragrance of sweet osmanthus drifted into my room.

I find it very difficult to get up in the morning. However, the fragrance of sweet osmanthus became my only morning pleasure. I came to enjoy getting up in the morning. The sky is beautiful, and I can also feel that I am alive. I feel it was such a missed opportunity, wondering why I had not been able to wake up every morning surrounded by the beautiful sky and the fragrance of flowers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.0: Until not long ago, I felt reluctant to accept a seat offered to me on a train or bus.
Until…; は emphasizes the time boundary in contrast with the present.
Passive form: 席を譲られる means to be offered someone else's seat.
To feel resistance or reluctance toward doing or experiencing something; こと nominalizes the action.
Describes an ongoing psychological state in the past.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.1: I used to make a point of standing in front of people who were sleeping or reading.
Lists representative actions, here sleeping or reading; it does not require one person to do both.
Used to make a conscious effort to do something; here, deliberately choosing where to stand to avoid being offered a seat.
This describes how the writer avoided being offered a seat, not the reason for the reluctance; it rules out option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.2: Yet recently, more and more people have been offering me their seats.
Someone does something beneficial for the speaker; here, offering the writer a seat.
Describes a change developing up to the present: the number of people offering seats has increased.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.3: At seventy, however young I always think I am, I suppose that to those around me I must clearly be an elderly person.
In 70歳の自分では, presents the writer's circumstances: being seventy years old.
To consider oneself to be…; 若いつもり expresses a self-perception of being young, rather than an intention.
Even if…; contrasts the writer's self-perception with how others see the writer.
From the perspective of…; in the eyes of…
Must be…; expresses a strongly held conclusion.
Probably…; expresses an explanatory conjecture, here as the writer's reflection.
The writer always felt young, supporting the inference that the writer previously did not want to be seen as elderly.
In contrast to the writer's self-image, others see the writer as elderly. Being offered a seat brings this into focus, supporting answer 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.4: When I was young, I never imagined that growing older would bring me happiness.
did not do; here: did not imagine
When…; establishes a time and contrasts youth with the present.
To find happiness in…; 年齢を重ねる means to grow older.
Never even imagined that…; と marks the imagined content, while は and も emphasize how unexpected it was.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.sentences.5: I think that now being able to express my gratitude openly and take a seat is proof that I have come to accept aging.
In 表現し、, し is the connective stem of する, linking expressing gratitude with taking a seat.
Potential forms: 座れる means can sit; 受け入れられた here means was able to accept.
Has become able to…; here it describes a psychological change allowing the writer to accept an offered seat.
Nominalizes an event as the topic, then explains or evaluates it.
I think that…; presents the writer's judgment.
The writer now accepts aging, reinforcing the inference that the earlier reluctance came from not wanting to be regarded as elderly.
Expressing gratitude and accepting a seat are changes following acceptance of aging, rather than the underlying reason suggested in option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.l: Earlier reluctance to accept a seat
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.n: The writer used to resist accepting a seat and deliberately stood in front of sleeping or reading passengers. This avoidance behavior helps rule out option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.l: Feeling young but being seen as elderly
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.n: More people now offer the writer a seat. The contrast between feeling young and being seen as elderly reveals the earlier wish not to be regarded as elderly, supporting answer 1.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.2.n: The writer discovers happiness in growing older. Expressing gratitude and taking a seat demonstrate acceptance of aging and help explain the earlier attitude.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.outline.3.n: Explains 証し through the related words 証拠 and 証明.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t32-p1.vietnamese:
Until not long ago, I felt reluctant to accept a seat offered to me on a train or bus. I used to make a point of standing in front of people who were sleeping or reading.

Yet recently, more and more people have been offering me their seats. At seventy, however young I always think I am, I suppose that to those around me I must clearly be an elderly person.

When I was young, I never imagined that growing older would bring me happiness. I think that now being able to express my gratitude openly and take a seat is proof that I have come to accept aging.

(Note) 証し: evidence; proof.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.0: My daughter, a university student, works at a family restaurant.
Describes ongoing employment: the daughter currently works at the restaurant.
The particle で marks the place where someone works.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.1: She had no experience dealing with customers, and she seemed nervous at first.
Means to deal with or serve someone; here, it refers to working with customers.
なく is the connective form of ない, linking the lack of experience to the following clause.
Means someone seemed to have been in a certain state. The narrator infers that the daughter was nervous at first.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.2: On one occasion, my daughter apparently forgot to note down one customer's order and apologized to the customer.
Attaches to a verb's ます-stem to mean forgetting to do something; here, 取り忘れる means forgetting to write something down.
The connective form of ～てしまう, expressing an unintended action with regret.
Reports something the narrator has heard; here, it conveys the daughter's account.
Identifies the daughter's mistake, corresponding to ミスして in the title in answer 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.3: However, the customer instead encouraged her, saying, “The work is hard, but please have confidence in yourself.”
Means “although” or “but,” linking the difficulty of the job to the encouragement to be confident.
Expresses a polite request or advice; here, it encourages the daughter to be confident.
Marks the quoted words accompanying the verb 励ます.
Describes someone doing something beneficial for the speaker or someone close to them; here, the customer encourages the daughter.
Directly supports answer 3: the daughter made a mistake and received encouragement, rather than scolding or praise.
This is advice to be confident, not confirmation that the daughter became confident, so answer 4 is unsupported.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.4: A few months later, the customer reportedly visited the restaurant again and kindly asked her, “Have you gotten used to the work?”
Means to get used to something; に marks what someone becomes accustomed to.
A polite question about a past action or an attained state; here, it asks whether she has become accustomed to the work.
Reports that someone kindly did something for the speaker or someone close to them; here, the customer checked in on the daughter.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.5: My daughter was delighted and said she was grateful for that kind thoughtfulness.
The past form of an い-adjective: ありがたい → ありがたかった.
Describes being delighted, with と marking the accompanying thought or statement.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.sentences.6: Through working in society, my daughter is learning from a variety of experiences.
Nominalizes a dictionary-form verb: 働くこと means the act of working.
Means through an activity or process; here, working allows the daughter to learn from experience.
Describes an ongoing process of learning.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.outline.0.l: A new job and initial nerves
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.outline.0.n: The narrator's daughter works at a family restaurant and initially seems nervous because she has no experience dealing with customers.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.outline.1.n: The daughter forgets to note an order and apologizes. The customer instead encourages her to be confident. This central event establishes answer 3 as the best title.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.outline.2.n: The customer returns and asks whether she has become used to the job; she is delighted and grateful for the thoughtfulness.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.outline.3.n: The narrator observes that the daughter is learning from various experiences through working in society.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
My daughter, a university student, works at a family restaurant. She had no experience dealing with customers, and she seemed nervous at first.

On one occasion, she told me she had forgotten to note down one customer's order and had apologized to the customer. However, the customer instead encouraged her, saying, “The work is hard, but please have confidence in yourself.” A few months later, the customer apparently visited the restaurant again and kindly asked her, “Have you gotten used to the work?” My daughter was delighted and said she was grateful for that kind thoughtfulness.

Through working in society, my daughter is learning from a variety of experiences.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t34-p1.sentences.0: I think we should make an effort to read plenty of books while we are young.
While a condition still holds; 若いうちに means “while still young,” before that stage passes.
Make an effort to do something or establish a habit; here, reading books.
Should do something. 読むようにしたほうがいい recommends making a habit of reading.
I think that…; introduces the writer’s opinion.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t34-p1.sentences.1: At first, I thought spending time reading was wasteful, but in sixth grade, I read a book for elementary school children that my grandmother had bought me, and my view changed.
book (as defined in the passage’s note)
Expresses a view held during an earlier period.
But…; contrasts the initial view with the later change.
At the time of…; 小学6年生の時に identifies the time as the writer’s sixth-grade year.
Someone did something for the speaker’s benefit; the grandmother bought the writer a book.
Intended for a particular audience; 小学生向け means intended for elementary school children.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: 祖母が買ってくれた modifies 小学生向け文庫本.
読んで links reading the book to the resulting change in perspective.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t34-p1.sentences.2: The print was large, and there were plenty of illustrations, so I was able to enjoy reading it.
An い-adjective takes the く form to connect clauses: 大きい → 大きく.
Adds another feature: besides large print, the book also had many illustrations; あって connects to the following clause.
The く form of an adjective describes how an action is performed: 楽しく読む means to read with enjoyment.
Was able to do something; the past form of ～ことができる.
Provides an explanation for the writer’s change of perspective in the preceding sentence.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t34-p1.sentences.3: You may think books are boring because they have no moving images or sound.
Lists representative examples: images and sound.

default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t48-p1.vietnamese:
Free Provision of Surplus Items Remaining in Former Government Buildings

Date & Time: February 26 (Sat) & February 27 (Sun), 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM
* Advance registration is required. However, the period from February 14 (Mon) through February 21 (Mon) and weekends are excluded.

Locations: Former Yatabe Office, Former Sakura Office, Former Tsukuba Office, Former Kukizaki Office

Details: Following the relocation of government offices in May of last year, surplus items no longer in use, such as lockers and office desks, are being offered free of charge. While efforts were made to repurpose items previously used in former government buildings for the city hall and local branch agencies as much as possible, a substantial number still remains.

Eligibility: Public organizations consisting of two or more citizens residing, working, or studying in the city, whose primary location of activity is within the city (volunteer groups, non-profit organizations, neighborhood/ward associations, children's clubs, etc.).
* Individuals are not eligible.
* The buildings are scheduled to be open for preview on February 10 (Thu) from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Carrying items out of the premises is strictly prohibited.
* For further details, please consult the city website or contact us.

Inquiries: Property Management Division

default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t49-p1.vietnamese:
To all foreigners living in Japan

How to Take a Bath

In Japan, there is a custom of getting into a large bath together with many people. Japanese baths are not only for cleaning the body, but also serve as a place for communication, such as having a relaxing chat in the bathtub, and can be said to be a part of culture. Please refer to the etiquette below and definitely enjoy bathing in Japan.

■ Wash your body thoroughly before getting into the bathtub

■ Do not wash your body or put soap into the bathtub

■ Do not put towels into the bathtub

■ Do not do laundry in the washing area

※ Those with long hair should tie it up with a rubber band or similar so that their hair does not soak in the bathwater

※ Make sure that water or hot water does not splash onto other people
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.0: Marks the addressee at the beginning of a letter or notice: to…
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.1: Points to keep in mind when looking for accommodation
Dictionary-form verb + ための + noun: something intended for a particular purpose.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.2: 1. If you cannot hold everyday conversations in Japanese, private accommodation is difficult to rent.
If one does not…; introduces a usual consequence of a condition not being met.
Attaches to the verb stem to express difficulty. Difficult to rent does not mean impossible to rent.
Rules out option 4: the text says renting is difficult, not impossible.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.3: To rent private accommodation, you must discuss matters in Japanese with a real estate agent or landlord.
In order to…; introduces what is necessary to achieve a goal.
Must…; replace ない in the negative form with なければならない to express necessity.
Lists representative examples without necessarily exhausting all possibilities.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.4: In this situation, ask a Japanese friend or a senior student who is good at Japanese to go and help you.
Have someone do something for you; に marks the person performing the action.
Links two actions done for the speaker; the volitional もらおう here offers advice to the reader.
A person who is good at…; の can replace が within a noun-modifying clause.
Rules out option 1: the text recommends help from a friend or senior student, but does not require an interpreter.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.5: 2. Commuting to school usually takes at least an hour.
Marks the activity under discussion: when it comes to commuting to school…
After a duration, は emphasizes a minimum: it takes at least that long.
Helps rule out option 2: the usual commute is at least an hour; the text does not guarantee accommodation 40 minutes away.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.6: Many people probably want to live close to school, but you should expect this to be difficult, especially if the school is in a business or commercial district.
Think that one would like to…; expresses a wish.
Probably…; a formal written equivalent of だろう expressing conjecture, here following 思う.
But…; contrasts the wish to live near school with the difficulty of doing so.
If; in the case that…; here introduces a condition concerning the school's location.
Should…; 思ったほうがよい advises adopting an expectation and does not describe past thinking.
Rules out option 2: living near a school in a business or commercial district is difficult; no 40-minute accommodation claim is made.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.7: 3. Signing a rental contract requires funds equivalent to roughly five to six months' rent.
Dictionary-form verb + には: to do…; introduces a necessary condition.
A specified number of months' worth; here, an amount equal to five to six months' rent.
Directly supports answer 3: signing the contract requires roughly five to six months' rent in expenses.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.sentences.8: When renting a home in Japan, you must prepare a total amount equivalent to roughly five to six months' rent, covering the security deposit, key money, agency fee, rent, and other expenses.
When…; identifies the situation in which the statement applies.
And so on; such as…; marks a non-exhaustive list.
Approximately a specified number of months' worth; here calculated using monthly rent.
Must…; here emphasizes the need to prepare the money.
Confirms answer 3: the combined required funds equal roughly five to six months' rent, rather than consisting solely of advance rent.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.outline.0.n: Introduces advice for international students looking for accommodation.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.outline.1.n: Limited Japanese conversation skills make private accommodation harder to rent. Discussions with an agent or landlord are necessary, and a Japanese friend or proficient senior student can help.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.outline.2.n: Commuting usually takes at least an hour. Living near school is difficult, especially in a business or commercial district.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.outline.3.n: Initial funds should total roughly five to six months' rent, including the deposit, key money, agency fee, and rent. This directly supports answer 3.
default.p.115dokkai_tanbun_n3-t50-p1.vietnamese:
To all international students

Points to keep in mind when looking for accommodation

1. If you cannot hold everyday conversations in Japanese, private accommodation is difficult to rent.

To rent private accommodation, you must discuss matters in Japanese with a real estate agent or landlord. In this situation, ask a Japanese friend or a senior student who is good at Japanese to go and help you.

2. Commuting to school usually takes at least an hour.

Many people probably want to live close to school, but you should expect this to be difficult, especially if the school is in a business or commercial district.

3. Signing a rental contract requires funds equivalent to roughly five to six months' rent.

When renting a home in Japan, you must prepare a total amount equivalent to roughly five to six months' rent, covering the security deposit, key money, agency fee, rent, and other expenses.
